def specs_from_file(path: Path) -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]]:
    """Return ``(label, spec)`` pairs from a spec or flepimop2 config file.

    Raises:
        RuntimeError: If PyYAML is not installed.
    """
    try:
        import yaml  # type: ignore[import-untyped]  # ruff: ignore[import-outside-top-level]
    except ImportError as exc:  # pragma: no cover - environment dependent
        msg = "op_system.validate needs PyYAML to read configuration files"
        raise RuntimeError(msg) from exc
    loaded = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) or {}
    systems = loaded.get("system") if isinstance(loaded, dict) else None
    if isinstance(systems, list):
        return [
            (f"{path}[system {index}]", dict(entry["spec"]))
            for index, entry in enumerate(systems)
            if isinstance(entry, dict) and entry.get("module") == "op_system"
        ]
    return [(str(path), dict(loaded))]

docs.title: Plan: jax.vmap over block-diagonal axes (factorize_axes)
docs.text: Status: ✅ complete 2026-05-28. All four slices merged. Naming: keep factorize_axes.

docs.title: 1. What's already true today
docs.text:
Layer Status op_system.compile_rhs Produces both eval_fn (flat) and pytree_eval_fn (StateDict → StateDict), plus template_shapes and a passthrough factorize_axes: tuple[str, ...] field. op_system vectorizer Already emits one shaped tensor expression per state template; factorize_axes is not consumed by the vectorizer — it is advisory metadata. flepimop2-op_system connector Exposes pytree_stepper_fn, template_shapes, factorize_axes, axis_order, axis_sizes, axis_labels, axis_coords on options. diffrax_engine.runner / runner_vmap One ODE solve per draw; runner_vmap already vmaps draws. No partitioning across model axes. Configs (SMH_R19_op_system*) FOI is per-loc (no cross-loc reads). All state templates contain loc. No params index loc except rho_h[loc], rho_d[loc] (used only in the observation likelihood, not the RHS).

So the runtime contract pytree_stepper_fn(t, {base: y}, **params) → {base: dy} is already block-diagonal-friendly if the RHS is structurally separable across the partition axis. The pieces that don't yet exist are: a structural separability check, declaration in the spec, and a vmap-over-partition-axis path in the engine.

docs.title: 2. Concept and contract
docs.text:
Introduce a single, narrow concept: a block axis — a model axis a such that for every state template the RHS at coord a=i depends only on values at coord a=i of every other buffer (state or param) that carries axis a, and on values at every coord of buffers that do not carry axis a.

This is exactly what allows

dy/dt = f(t, y)   →    dy[..., i, ...]/dt = f_i(t, y[..., i, ...])

and therefore allows the engine to evaluate f with jax.vmap(in_axes=axis_position) over coord i.

Reuse the existing factorize_axes spec field as the block axis declaration. It already round-trips through normalize → compile → connector. We just give it real semantics in op_system and a real consumer in the engine.

docs.title: 3.1 op_system — promote factorize_axes from advisory to checked
docs.text:
Goal: at compile time, prove the declared axes are block-diagonal in the IR; emit per-template metadata the engine can trust without re-inspecting the IR.

  1. New IR pass analyze_block_axes(rhs) -> BlockAxisReport in a new _block_axes.py:
  2. For each axis a in meta["factorize_axes"]:
    • For each equations_ir / aliases_ir expression: walk subscripts.
    • Reject if any apply_along(..., a=...) / sum_over(a) / Reduce mentions a (cross-coord reduction).
    • Reject if any subscript pins a to a literal coord (e.g. loc=AK) without that same coord being the equation's cell coord on a.
    • Reject if any subscript renames a to a fresh bound name and uses it elsewhere at a different cell coord (I[..., loc:l] * J[..., loc:m] with l != m).
    • Allow any expression that touches a only as the matching free position of the cell template, or never mentions a.
  3. Also walk the operators list so a kernel keyed on a is rejected statically.
  4. Classify each parameter the RHS reads as axis_kind ∈ {has_axis, lacks_axis} for each block axis. (Already available via time_varying_params + shaped_params axes tuples.)

  5. Output: BlockAxisInfo(name, size, state_axis_pos: dict[base, int], param_axis_pos: dict[name, int|None]).

  6. Wire into compile_rhs:

  7. Call analyze_block_axes(rhs) for axes in meta["factorize_axes"].
  8. On any failure: raise UnsupportedFeatureError with the specific equation/alias and offending subscript (fail loudly, like the existing vectorize bail).
  9. On success: attach to CompiledRhs as a new field block_axes: tuple[BlockAxisInfo, ...]. Keep it pickle-stable: plain dataclass with builtin types.

  10. Continue exposing factorize_axes as the raw tuple for backwards compat.

  11. Tests in tests/op_system/test_block_axes.py: separable RHS passes; cross-loc RHS rejects with named reason; mixed state where one template lacks the axis rejects; operator on partition axis rejects.

  12. Docs in docs/api-reference/specs.md: short section on block axes.

LOC estimate: ~400 src + ~250 tests.

docs.title: 3.2 flepimop2-op_system connector — publish the new info
docs.text:
src/flepimop2/system/op_system/__init__.py:

  1. Forward compiled.block_axes onto self.options["block_axes"].
  2. No behaviour change in _bind_impl.
  3. Tests in flepimop2-op_system/tests/test_system.py: round-trip for a config declaring factorize_axes: [loc]; empty otherwise.

LOC estimate: ~30 src + ~50 tests.

docs.title: 3.3 diffrax_engine — implement the partitioned solve
docs.text:
COVID19_USA/model_input/plugins/diffrax_engine.py:

  1. _prepare_call extension: read stepper.option("block_axes"). Pick one block axis for the run via a new opt key block_solve_axis (default: first entry of block_axes; None disables). Stash on prep as block_axis: BlockAxisInfo | None.

  2. New solve closure when block_axis is set and we are on the pytree path:

  3. Build _solve_one_block over the sliced state dict + sliced params.
  4. _solve = jax.vmap(_solve_one_block, in_axes=(per_base_axis_pos, per_param_axis_pos)) — positions from block_axis.state_axis_pos / block_axis.param_axis_pos (None ⇒ broadcast). Use out_axes so vmap re-inserts at the original axis position.

  5. The inner _solve_one_block calls pytree_stepper_fn with the sliced state_dict and sliced params; diffrax solves a much smaller ODE.

  6. runner semantics: pytree return is still {base: (T, *full_shape)} — vmap reinserts the block axis automatically (use out_axes to land it at the original position; no reshape needed).

  7. runner_vmap semantics: nest as jax.vmap(draws, jax.vmap(block_axis, _solve_one_block)). Static signatures already match across draws, so the existing "same _solve" guard still works.

  8. Operator-splitting (_make_advection_term_pytree, _make_jump_term_pytree): build operator terms inside _solve_one_block (after slicing) so they see the per-block shapes.

  9. Fallback / safety:

  10. If block_axes is empty or pytree_mode is False: behave exactly as today (no regression).

  11. If a param the engine routes as dynamic carries the block axis but block_axis.param_axis_pos[name] is None: raise clearly.

  12. Tests in COVID19_USA/tests/test_diffrax_engine.py:

  13. Numerical equivalence: monolithic solve vs. block-partitioned solve on a tiny 2-loc separable config — must match to solver tolerance.
  14. Shape contract: runner output dict has correct full shapes.
  15. Negative: monolithic-only config (no factorize_axes) still passes through unmodified.

LOC estimate: ~350 src + ~200 tests.

docs.title: 3.4 Configs — opt in
docs.text:
In each config that should solve per-location, add at the spec level:

spec:
  kind: transitions
  factorize_axes: [loc]
  axes: ...

No other config changes needed — FOI is already loc-local in the continuum configs.

docs.title: 3.5 flepimop2 core — no changes
docs.text: flepimop2's EngineProtocol.runner / runner_vmap signatures are unchanged. No core flepimop2 edits.

docs.title: 4. Order of work
docs.text:
1. op_system: analyze_block_axes + CompiledRhs.block_axes + tests.
  2. Connector: forward block_axes to options + tests.
  3. diffrax_engine: partitioned _solve_one_block + numerical-equivalence test.
  4. Opt configs into factorize_axes: [loc] and run prior-predictive smoke.

docs.title: 5. Risks and open questions
docs.text:
• Operator terms with non-local kernels on the block axis: the separability analyzer rejects these — IR walk must include the operators list.
  • runner_vmap × block-vmap memory: vmapping draws outside and block-axis inside means the inner solve has shapes (D, n_loc, ...). Same total work as today but XLA may pick a different schedule; benchmark on GPU before committing nesting order.
  • Multiple block axes: spec already accepts a list. v1: support exactly one runtime block axis (pick first; engine opt overrides). Multi-axis nesting is a follow-up.

docs.title: Citation and archiving
docs.text:
Use the repository's CITATION.cff to credit the software. The record describes the shared op_system and flepimop2-op_system release and retains the authors/order from the two package metadata files. Core is MIT-licensed; the adapter is GPLv3-or-later licensed. Record both distribution versions when using the adapter, plus backend and flepimop2 versions needed to reproduce the calculation.

For published work, cite the exact version used and its release URL. A citation for version 0.7.0 can identify Joshua Macdonald, Carl Pearson, and Timothy Willard, op_system: RHS specification compiler and flepimop2 provider, version 0.7.0, released 2026-10-06, with the v0.7.0 release. For a development checkout, also record the commit and any local modifications. Do not label unreleased behavior as part of 0.7.0 merely because the package version has not yet been bumped. Use the CFF in the tag when one is available; the first CFF here documents the already released 0.7.0 metadata.

Validate syntax with just citation, which uses the isolated, pinned cffconvert validator for CFF 1.2.0. Maintainers review attribution rather than deriving authors from commit counts. Update version, date-released, and the release artifact URL alongside a shared version bump; citation checks enforce consistency with package metadata and the dated changelog. No preferred paper citation is currently recorded. Add preferred-citation after a paper's authors, title, venue, year, and persistent identifier are verified; retain the software version citation for reproducibility.

docs.title: Current identifier audit
docs.text: On 2026-10-13, the repository, publication workflows, and public GitHub release notes recorded no archive DOI, .zenodo.json, or Zenodo integration instructions. A DataCite query for the exact repository URL returned no records; public web searches found none. The Zenodo API request timed out. These observations do not establish that no archive exists: a maintainer's connected Zenodo account and unindexed records cannot be verified from this checkout. No DOI is invented in CITATION.cff, and the current publication workflow creates GitHub releases and package-index artifacts without itself performing an archival deposit.

docs.title: Software-paper release archive plan
docs.text:
The maintainer has selected the ACCIDDA Zenodo archive for the software-paper release. The archival deposit and resolving DOI still need verification. Complete the JOSS readiness milestone before freezing the archive release.

Before a paper release, the release maintainer must check existing archive records and the repository's connected archival account. Reuse the established record/version series if one exists; avoid minting a duplicate identifier for the same release. If none exists, select one maintained archive such as Zenodo and establish its GitHub release integration or perform a documented manual deposit. See Zenodo's repository integration and release archive instructions.

The paper release should then follow this sequence:

  1. Confirm attribution, licenses, shared version, release date, changelog, and citation metadata. Run just ci, just qualify, and just release-validate.
  2. Tag and publish the shared release through the existing workflow. Archive the exact tagged source for both distributions, their released artifacts, and any benchmark JSON/fixtures used for paper claims. Retain the tag/commit, checksums, environment versions, and links to versioned docs.
  3. Verify that the archival record resolves and contains that exact release. Record its version DOI in the release notes and citation metadata; if the archive provides a concept DOI, identify it separately as the version series. Use the version DOI for a reproducible software-paper release citation.
  4. Link the verified archive from the paper and release notes. Add a verified preferred paper citation when published. Check identifiers and CFF syntax again before announcing the release.

This plan records work for the release maintainer. Adding this guidance does not create a deposit, enable an integration, or reserve an identifier. The shared GitHub release URL remains the verified identifier until an archive is confirmed.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text: This page captures conventions adopted across op_system. They are not strict rules — exceptions exist where the trade-offs differ — but new code should follow them by default and call out any deviation in the PR description.

docs.title: Records: NamedTuple vs @dataclass
docs.text:
op_system parsers and normalizers produce many small "value records": parsed selectors, normalized axes, validated constraint rules, compiled kernel descriptors, etc. For these we have a default and a fallback.

Default to typing.NamedTuple for small, value-like records that are produced once by a parser and read many times.

Reasons:

  • Immutable — downstream code cannot silently mutate the record.
  • Hashable — usable as dict keys and in sets without extra work.
  • Tuple-compatible — legacy unpacking (base, tokens = parse_selector(s)) keeps working and NamedTuple records compare equal to plain tuples of the same values.
  • Zero boilerplate — fields and types in one declaration, no __init__ required.

Use @dataclass (preferably @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)) when you need any of:

  • Mutability.
  • field(default_factory=...) for mutable defaults.
  • __post_init__ validation that cannot live in a parser/classmethod.
  • Inheritance.
  • Keyword-only construction (@dataclass(kw_only=True)).
  • Computed fields beyond what a from_* classmethod would express.

docs.title: Colocate parsers with the type they produce
docs.text: Whenever a record has a non-trivial parsing/validation path, expose it as a classmethod on the record type — typically from_string, from_mapping, or from_yaml_node. The pattern is modeled on ParsedShorthand.from_string in flepimop2._utils._module. This keeps the constructor of record next to the spec for what a valid record looks like.

docs.title: Internal vs public names
docs.text:
Modules whose name starts with an underscore (_axes, _constraints, _helpers, _normalize, _symbols, _templates) are internal to op_system. Types and helpers defined in those modules should also be underscore-prefixed unless they are deliberately re-exported from a public module (e.g. op_system.specs, op_system.compile, the package __init__).

This applies to record classes too: an internal record produced by a private parser is _ConstraintRule, not ConstraintRule. Promoting an internal type to public should be a deliberate decision tied to a stability commitment.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Raise the specific exception type at the point of failure rather than delegating to a _raise_* helper. The shared exception types live in op_system._errors:

  • InvalidRhsSpecError(ValueError) — structural problems with a normalized RHS spec (missing fields, wrong types, unknown references).
  • InvalidExpressionError(ValueError) — expression strings that fail parsing/AST validation.
  • UnsupportedFeatureError(NotImplementedError) — features declared in a spec that are not yet implemented.

All three subclass a built-in (ValueError / NotImplementedError), so existing except ValueError / except NotImplementedError sites in downstream code keep working while new code can catch the more specific subclasses when needed.

Document the specific exception type in the function's Raises: block.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
The repository's contributor guide covers clean setup, compiler/provider boundaries, focused behavior tests, required local checks, wheel verification, support, and releases.

Run baseline just ci, mandatory CPU backend just qualify, and installed-wheel just build-all checks before pushing a PR. Optional GPU and large benchmark runs are separate from that required matrix. The code conventions, backend qualification guide, and numerical qualification guide give the contracts those checks protect.

For versioned citations and the software-paper archive plan, see citation and archiving. Maintainers publish both distributions together through the release workflow.

docs.title: Readiness coverage audit
docs.text:
This audit maps compiler and provider behavior to current regression tests. The tests protect observable contracts; the table does not claim 100% line or branch coverage or numerical validity of every user model.

Paths below are relative to the repository root. Source and installed-wheel suites exercise these contracts; mandatory backend jobs additionally reject missing or skipped selected tests. See contributing for the local commands and backend qualification for the qualified CPU precision, layout, and AD boundaries.

Requested area Evidence Mixing kernel generation flepimop2-op_system/tests/test_mixing_kernels.py: independent scalar formulas for all five forms, rectangular source/target grids, one-axis square grids, custom asymmetric matrix orientation, scalar no-axis policy, flat/structured injection with independent nonuniform quadrature. test_erfc_kernel.py checks fixed numerical values and positive tails. Multi-axis and categorical/ordinal/continuous axes tests/op_system/test_op_system_specs.py, test_op_system_templates.py, test_time_interpolation.py: generated linear/log grids, coordinate validation, multi-axis selectors, pinned coordinates and singleton time axes. test_axis_edge_contracts.py rejects empty coordinate lists for each type while retaining scalar axes: []. Sum and integration helpers test_op_system_apply_along.py, test_op_system_ir_lower.py, test_renewal_births.py: helper composition, filters, categorical sums, trapezoidal weights, mismatched axis-type errors, and births. Required test_backend_qualification.py checks nested mixed categorical/continuous reductions against an analytic bilinear integral on nonuniform grids, including precision and JAX/Torch derivatives. Hazard-rate transitions and conservation test_routing_transitions.py, test_axis_kernel.py, test_jump_integral.py, test_renewal_births.py: independently computed cell flows, batch balance, source/target orientation and open/closed-system invariants. Required backend cases compare independent block, mixed-selector and global-total flows. Provider construction and metadata flepimop2-op_system/tests/test_system.py: bind/step interfaces, flat/structured/block parity, flatten/unflatten helpers, axis order/sizes/coordinates/types/labels, parameter requests, time tables, operators and reactions. test_sparse_table.py covers support assembly. scripts/qualify_provider_types.py gates the installed wheel's public types. Failure paths test_op_system_specs.py, test_op_system_compile.py, test_bare_state_references.py, test_mixed_template_selectors.py: malformed declarations, missing/indexed states, allowlisted ASTs and legacy-selector diagnostics. Provider kernel tests check unknown axes/forms, missing form parameters and missing custom values.

The audit exposed and separately fixed unavailable numpy.erfc, untyped literal precision, and incompatible/promoting continuous weights. The broader inventory therefore checks actual matrix values and derivative behavior rather than accepting compilation or metadata shape alone.

Gamma kernels retain their existing unnormalized shape with distance clipped to 1e-12 at zero. No-axis analytic declarations retain scalar params.value (default zero); callers must declare axes to obtain a generated matrix. Cross-axis constraints are preserved as reserved metadata by public normalization; private parser tests do not establish public validation or masking. Constraint-based filtering and reductions remain unimplemented. Optional GPU paths and large timing runs are not qualified by the required CPU matrix.

docs.title: Creating A Release
docs.text:
This guide covers the op_system release process for this repository's two Python distributions:

  • op_system
  • flepimop2-op_system

The release workflow treats them as a single release unit. Both package versions must match, and the workflow publishes them sequentially under one GitHub release tag.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You have write access to the ACCIDDA/op_system repository.
  • The release version has already been updated everywhere it is declared:
  • pyproject.toml
  • flepimop2-op_system/pyproject.toml
  • CITATION.cff has matching version, release date, and artifact URL, with maintainer-reviewed attribution from the package metadata.
  • The CHANGELOG.md has a section for the new version.
  • Your local environment is synced with a supported Python version.
  • You have GitHub's gh CLI installed and authenticated if you plan to dispatch workflows from the command line.

docs.title: 1. Confirm The Shared Version
docs.text:
The release workflow validates that all version declarations match before it builds or publishes anything.

Today that means these two files must contain the same semantic version:

  • pyproject.toml
  • flepimop2-op_system/pyproject.toml

If they differ, the validate job fails immediately. Both public module versions are read dynamically from installed package metadata, using the distribution names op_system and flepimop2-op-system, so neither needs a separate manual edit. The provider reports 0+unknown only when imported directly from an uninstalled source tree where distribution metadata is absent.

docs.title: 2. Run The Local Release Preflight
docs.text:
Use the local pre-release target before dispatching the release workflow:

just release-validate

That command performs these checks:

  • Validates CFF syntax and checks citation attribution, shared version, date, and release URL against package metadata and the dated changelog.

  • Validates that the release version matches in:

  • pyproject.toml
  • flepimop2-op_system/pyproject.toml
  • Runs just build-all to execute the clean-room build and install tests for both packages.

The release workflow runs the same validation again on GitHub Actions before publishing.

docs.title: 3. Run The Release Workflow
docs.text:
Releases are created through the manual GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/release.yaml.

If you are testing the workflow before merging, add --ref <branch-name> to the gh workflow run command. Without --ref, GitHub dispatches the workflow definition from the repository's default branch.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Use this to validate shared versioning, build both packages, and upload release artifacts without publishing anything:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/op_system \
  --ref <branch-name> \
  --field publish-target=none \
  --field create-github-release=false \
  --field deploy-docs=false

This runs the validate, publish-core, and publish-provider jobs, but the publish jobs become no-ops when publish-target=none.

docs.title: TestPyPI
docs.text:
Use this to publish both packages to TestPyPI without creating the GitHub release or deploying docs:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/op_system \
  --ref <branch-name> \
  --field publish-target=testpypi \
  --field create-github-release=false \
  --field deploy-docs=false

The workflow always publishes in dependency order:

  1. op_system
  2. flepimop2-op_system

When testing from a branch, keep create-github-release=false and deploy-docs=false. The reusable docs workflow checks out main, so it is not intended for pre-merge branch testing.

docs.title: PyPI
docs.text:
Use this to publish both packages, create a GitHub release, and deploy the versioned documentation:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/op_system \
  --field publish-target=pypi \
  --field create-github-release=true \
  --field deploy-docs=true

When create-github-release=true, the workflow creates a single vX.Y.Z GitHub release for the shared package version and uses GitHub's generated release notes.

docs.title: 4. Documentation Deployment
docs.text:
The release workflow calls .github/workflows/gh-pages.yaml as a reusable workflow when deploy-docs=true.

That workflow supports two deployment modes:

  • push: for normal main branch documentation updates
  • release: for a tagged release, which updates the release alias in mike

If you want to deploy docs manually without running a release, you can dispatch gh-pages.yaml directly and choose the deploy mode in the GitHub Actions UI.

docs.title: 5. Trusted Publishing Setup
docs.text:
The publish jobs use PyPI Trusted Publishing rather than a stored API token.

For publish-target=testpypi, configure the TestPyPI trusted publisher entry for:

  • Owner: ACCIDDA
  • Repository: op_system
  • Workflow file: release.yaml

For publish-target=pypi, configure the PyPI trusted publisher entry for the same repository and workflow file.

Because this repository publishes two distributions from one workflow, the same trusted publisher setup must be allowed to publish both package names on the selected index.

docs.title: 6. Current Packaging Note
docs.text: The release workflow now handles the mechanics of validating, building, and sequencing both distributions together. Package-index acceptance still depends on the metadata inside each built distribution, so publishing flepimop2-op_system to a public index may still require follow-up packaging changes outside the workflow itself.

docs.title: 7. Software-Paper Archive
docs.text: GitHub release and package publishing do not themselves confirm an archival deposit. Follow the citation and archiving plan: verify existing arrangements before creating a new record, archive the exact shared release, and record a verified version DOI and any distinct concept DOI. The paper should identify the tagged software and its independently retained benchmark/environment evidence.

docs.title: Compiler execution and export roadmap
docs.text: Engineering decisions recorded on 2026-10-21. Planned work does not expand the qualified backend surface. The shared execution roadmap and baseline protocol describe cross-package ownership and measurements.

docs.title: Keep the public numerical contract
docs.text:
Retain Python model interfaces and namespace discovery from input arrays. Keep NumPy, JAX and CPU Torch qualification. CuPy/CUDA is the next explicit end-to-end target, not an implication of Array API compatibility. Sparse operators, compilation, differentiation and device support have separate contracts.

Generated vectorized expression functions are already cached without per-expression runtime eval. Measure normalization, compilation and evaluator layouts before choosing an acceleration target. Optional Numba needs a supported generated function signature; decorating an arbitrary dynamic Python closure is insufficient. An explicitly requested unavailable/unsupported accelerator must produce a clear result, rather than silently appearing to use that accelerator.

docs.title: Compiler-owned work
docs.text:
Work Scope and dependency Structural model identity Versioned canonical content serialization with ordered state/parameter/coordinate layouts, expressions, observables, constants and relevant compilation/view options. Separate structural identity from fitted values and runtime identity. Do not change object equality/hash behavior incidentally. Derivative exports Reuse checked dependency structure. State and parameter derivatives and observable derivatives have distinct shapes and meanings. Unsupported IR operations fail explicitly; qualify small dense values/actions independently before general sparse or matrix-free claims. IR export Versioned typed serialization and a bounded Julia emitter with explicit supported rational/expression semantics. Export remains separate from normal evaluation. Numba experiment Optional NumPy-only lowering, chosen after representative baseline measurements; report compilation and amortized execution costs and preserve reference behavior. Rust/PyO3 IR experiment Deferred private implementation of normalization/tree passes, preserving Python IR/public contracts; enter after compile-time profiles or external-runtime consumers justify it.

Julia export serves optional external structural-identifiability tools; it does not start a full Julia port. A future C/LLVM emitter is another separately scoped consumer, not an automatic consequence of serializing the IR. No Rust rewrite of the small Python array protocol is planned.

docs.title: Reuse existing artifacts
docs.text:
Scaling-gauge declarations, bounded detection, verified outputs and anchored coordinate maps already exist. Inference consumers should reuse them rather than reimplement detection. Reported gauge rank or remaining parameter-coordinate count does not establish structural identifiability. Initial conditions, observation and noise parameters can change the statistical dimension.

Latent observables already compile separately from statistical measurement noise. OP Engine owns numerical observation evaluation/reduction; OP Infer owns shared sampling/log-density, censoring and prior semantics. Keep this boundary when qualifying a complete compiled simulation-to-observation workflow.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text: First reconcile open work and run the existing hierarchical compiler baseline. Develop structural identity and forward-consumer contracts early. Derivative and IR export work can proceed alongside shared observation/prior interfaces. Qualify JAX execution and explicit GPU cases before selecting additional native kernels. Revisit Rust normalization only after those measurements and contracts stabilize.

docs.title: Block-stripped pytree_eval_fn design record
docs.text:
Historical implementation plan. For current interfaces and supported layouts, use the getting-started guide. Tracker references below record the development context, not installation requirements.

Repo: ACCIDDA/op_system Branch convention: feat/168-<slug> Filed: 2026-05-28 Depends on: PRs from #162 / #158 / #156 already merged on main.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
pytree_eval_fn is rank-rigid. Its lowered body contains literal axis indices (np.transpose(buf, (2, 0, 1)), np.sum(buf, axis=k), alias-buffer reshapes). When diffrax_engine wraps it in jax.vmap(in_axes=<block_axis_pos>), vmap traces it on per-block slices where the block axis is missing → axis k out of bounds for array of dimension k-1 from inside an alias body.

analyze_block_axes already proves the block axis is separable, so stripping it is well-defined.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Add a second compiled function block_pytree_eval_fn on CompiledRhs that operates on block-stripped state. Engine swaps to it under vmap. Stripping logic lives in op_system, not the engine.

docs.title: Slice 1 — feat/168-strip-block-axis-ir
docs.text:
Goal: IR-level "strip a block axis" primitive + unit tests.

  • New src/op_system/_normalize_block.py:
  • strip_block_axis(rhs: ExprRhs | TransitionsRhs, axis_name: str) -> ExprRhs | TransitionsRhs
  • Walks equations_ir, aliases_ir, state_templates, shaped_params, time_varying_params.
  • Deletes axis_name from every shape tuple; rebuilds axis_order.
  • Strips coord-pinned subscripts on axis_name ([loc:l] → bare scalar slice).
  • Drops Reduce nodes whose axis is axis_name (already proven absent by analyze_block_axes; assert).
  • Refuses if axis_name is not in the spec axes.
  • Tests in tests/op_system/test_block_axes.py:
  • test_strip_block_axis_removes_axis_from_template_shapes
  • test_strip_block_axis_removes_axis_from_alias_bodies
  • test_strip_block_axis_strips_tv_param_axes (beta[time, loc] → beta[time])
  • test_strip_block_axis_raises_on_unknown_axis

Files: _normalize_block.py (new), tests/op_system/test_block_axes.py Dependencies: none. Budget: ~250 LOC.

docs.title: Slice 2 — feat/168-block-compile-pass
docs.text:
Goal: Wire stripping into compile_rhs; surface block_pytree_eval_fn + block_template_shapes.

  • src/op_system/_vectorize.py:
  • After existing flat + pytree compile, if compiled.block_axes is non-empty AND pytree_eval_fn is not None:
    1. stripped = strip_block_axis(rhs, block_axes[0].name)
    2. Run _lower_to_pytree_eval_fn(stripped, ...) → block_pytree_eval_fn
    3. Compute block_template_shapes from stripped state_templates.
  • Attach both to CompiledRhs (new fields, default None).
  • src/op_system/compile.py:
  • @dataclass add block_pytree_eval_fn: PytreeEvalFn | None = None
  • @dataclass add block_template_shapes: dict[str, tuple[int, ...]] | None = None
  • tests/op_system/test_block_axes.py:
  • test_compile_emits_block_pytree_eval_fn_when_block_axes_nonempty
  • test_block_pytree_eval_fn_matches_monolithic_at_each_block_coord
    • Compile SIR-like spec with factorize_axes: [loc].
    • Pick random y_full shape (age, vax, loc).
    • For each i: vmap(block_eval, in_axes=loc_pos)(y_full)[base][i] ≈ pytree_eval_fn(y_full)[base][..., i, ...] (within 1e-12).
  • test_compile_no_block_axes_leaves_block_fields_none

Files: _vectorize.py, compile.py, tests/op_system/test_block_axes.py Dependencies: Slice 1 merged. Budget: ~300 LOC.

docs.title: Slice 3 — feat/168-engine-uses-block-fn ✅ DONE
docs.text:
Goal: Switch diffrax_engine to use block_pytree_eval_fn; delete the engine-side stripping helper.

This slice lands in ACCIDDA/COVID19_USA, not op_system.

What was done: - model_input/plugins/diffrax_engine.py: - Merged _build_operator_terms_pytree_block into _build_operator_terms_pytree (added block_axis_name: str | None = None parameter); deleted the separate 80-LOC block function. - Block path now reads stepper.option("block_template_shapes") (from Slice 4 shim) instead of computing shapes inline. - Replaced else pytree_stepper_fn fallback with a RuntimeError assertion — block_pytree_stepper_fn must be set when entering the block path. - Acceptance gate (SMH_R19_op_system_hierarchical.yml -t prior_predictive) passes: EXIT=0. - tests/test_diffrax_engine.py: - _MockStepper now exposes block_pytree_stepper_fn and block_template_shapes from compiled.*. - All 4 existing tests pass with the real block_pytree_eval_fn path (no fallback).

Files: COVID19_USA model_input/plugins/diffrax_engine.py, tests/test_diffrax_engine.py Dependencies: Slice 2 released (op_system version bump). Budget: ~150 LOC of net deletes + ~80 LOC of new tests.

docs.title: Aging chains with coord_shift
docs.text:
A coord_shift transition moves mass along one axis of a state template. It has two forms.

The pairwise form moves one coordinate to another:

- coord_shift: {age: "a0 -> a1"}
  rate: aging_rate[age]
  apply_to: [S, I]

An aging chain over n bins needs n - 1 such entries. Each entry adds a masked term to every cell's equation, so the compile cost grows with the square of the number of bins. A named pairwise entry publishes one point-to- point reaction per state, named {name}_{state}.

The axis-wide form shifts every coordinate in a single entry:

- name: aging
  coord_shift: {axis: age, step: 1, rate: "aging_rate[age]", boundary: absorb}
  apply_to: [S, V, I, R]
  • step is a nonzero integer smaller in magnitude than the axis length. Bin k moves to bin k + step; step defaults to 1.
  • rate is a per-capita rate. A free age index in the rate, including one inside an alias or a state reference, reads the source bin. rate may appear inside coord_shift or on the transition, but not in both places.
  • boundary decides what happens to sources whose destination k + step falls off the axis. absorb removes that mass from the system (for example, culling at the oldest age). stay leaves it in place, giving an open-ended terminal bin. boundary has no default: omitting it, or writing error, rejects the spec and names the two alternatives.
  • Every apply_to state needs one state template with the shifted axis as a wildcard and no pinned coordinates. Other axes, such as vax or loc, are carried through unchanged.
import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec

ages = [f"a{k}" for k in range(4)]
spec = {
    "kind": "transitions",
    "axes": [{"name": "age", "type": "ordinal", "coords": ages}],
    "state": ["S[age]"],
    "transitions": [
        {
            "name": "aging",
            "coord_shift": {
                "axis": "age",
                "step": 1,
                "rate": "aging_rate[age]",
                "boundary": "absorb",
            },
            "apply_to": ["S"],
        }
    ],
}
compiled = compile_spec(spec)
rates = np.array([0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2])
s = np.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0])
flow = rates * s
expected = -flow
expected[1:] += flow[:-1]
np.testing.assert_allclose(compiled.eval_fn(0.0, s, aging_rate=rates), expected)

With boundary: stay the last bin keeps its mass, so expected[-1] would be flow[-2] and nothing would leave the system.

docs.title: Deterministic lowering
docs.text:
Each apply_to state lowers once, as matrix routing along the shifted axis with a synthesized one-hot shift matrix. Cell values equal those of the equivalent pairwise entries; for forward shifts they match bit for bit. Compile time no longer grows with the number of coordinate pairs: a 240-bin, four-state chain compiles in tens of milliseconds, compared with several seconds for 239 pairwise entries. Evaluation contracts the shift matrix, which costs O(n²) per template, the same order as the masked pairwise terms.

The shift matrix and the stay keep-mask are injected automatically under reserved __op_system_shift* names. They are not model parameters.

docs.title: Reaction artifacts
docs.text:
A named entry publishes one templated reaction per apply_to state, named {name}_{state} (aging_S above). The reaction does not have one pinned artifact per coordinate pair. Its propensity is shaped like the full template, with one channel per source cell:

(reaction,) = compiled.reactions
assert reaction.name == "aging_S"
assert reaction.from_axes == reaction.full_axes == ("age",)
assert reaction.to_axes == ()
assert reaction.sum_axes == reaction.pinned == ()
assert reaction.offsets == (("age", 1),)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    np.asarray(reaction.propensity_fn(0.0, {"S": s}, aging_rate=rates)), flow
)

The shifted axis appears in offsets, not in to_axes or pinned. A firing at source index k removes one unit from (S, k) and adds one to (S, k + step). Other destination axes are copied from to_axes and fixed by pinned as usual. When k + step is off the axis, the firing removes the unit and deposits nothing (absorb). Under stay, those sources have zero propensity, so they never fire.

A consumer that predates offsets fails its own metadata checks on these reactions. The destination axes no longer cover full_axes, so the reaction is rejected rather than silently treated as a no-op.

By default the reactants metadata is the consumed source alone. It is complete when the rate reads no state, as for a constant aging rate, and otherwise reports reactants_complete=False. One entry generates a reaction per apply_to state, so it cannot list each one's consumed source. Instead, declare the reactants beyond the shifted state as catalysts, or set catalysts: auto to infer them from the rate; catalysts: [] declares a first-order shift. The generator adds the consumed source, and each reaction reports reactants_complete=True, as adaptive tau-leaping requires. Both coord_shift forms accept catalysts and reject reactants.

docs.title: Array namespaces, engines, and providers
docs.text:
Use array namespace for the numerical array API resolved from input arrays by array_api_compat.array_namespace. “Array backend” is an equivalent term when discussing NumPy, JAX, or Torch. Use the qualified phrase when an engine or provider is also in the discussion.

Term Meaning in this repository Array namespace / array backend Array operations, dtype, and device selected by runtime state arrays Numerical engine A downstream integrator that advances the model in time, such as op_engine Provider / adapter Integration package exposing the core compiler through another framework, such as flepimop2-op_system Compiler op_system, which validates a specification and constructs reusable RHS evaluators

Compile a specification with compile_spec(spec), then provide NumPy arrays, JAX arrays/tracers, or Torch tensors when evaluating it. The specification and provider configuration do not select an array namespace. Parameters should use the qualified state's namespace and floating precision; see the qualification matrix for tested combinations. A JAX input selects JAX array operations; the caller still chooses whether to apply jax.jit, and the numerical engine chooses its integration method.

For flepimop2, system.module: op_system selects the system provider, while an engine module selects the numerical engine. Neither setting replaces the array namespace selected from the runtime state. The provider passes state arrays through without namespace coercion. Generated mixing matrices are constructed on the host during provider setup; their construction is a separate boundary from the runtime state namespace.

Existing compile_spec(backend=..., xp=...) and compile_rhs(xp=...) keyword arguments remain accepted, deprecated, and ignored. Their names are retained for compatibility, with the existing deprecation warnings. Remove these arguments and supply arrays of the desired namespace. No replacement array_backend configuration field is introduced: adding such a field would suggest compile-time selection that the current API does not perform. The provider has no namespace-selection backend setting; remove a legacy setting if present and configure runtime arrays through the consuming engine.

docs.title: Compiler backend qualification
docs.text:
op_system selects its numerical namespace from the input arrays. Optional runtime extras install JAX or Torch; installing the compiler alone requires neither. Root compiler qualification is a separate required CI matrix from the provider's tests and the baseline compiler test suite.

The required jobs explicitly install NumPy, JAX, or CPU Torch and execute the matching tests through scripts/qualify_backend.py. The runner fails if the backend is missing, if no tests run, or if a selected test is skipped. Ordinary optional-backend skips in the baseline suite therefore cannot substitute for these jobs.

docs.title: Qualified capabilities
docs.text:
The CI jobs run on Python 3.12 with the dependencies resolved for that run; their logs record backend and Python versions. Baseline package tests separately cover supported Python 3.11–3.13. Qualification covers float32 and float64 values, with JAX x64 enabled explicitly for double-precision checks. State and floating parameters use the same dtype; mixed-precision combinations remain unqualified.

Capability NumPy JAX CPU Torch Flat and structured/PyTree RHS parity, shapes, dtypes, namespace Qualified Qualified Qualified Independent-group block RHS Qualified, eager loop Qualified, eager loop and native vmap Qualified, eager loop and torch.func.vmap Coupled-group flat/structured RHS Qualified Qualified Qualified Treating coupled groups as independent blocks Rejected Rejected Rejected Native JIT and batched parameter evaluation No AD/JIT contract Qualified with jit/vmap Torch compiler integration unqualified Directional derivatives against independent finite differences No AD contract Qualified Autograd qualified in float64 CUDA/CuPy and other GPU execution Unqualified here Unqualified here Unqualified here

Named latent observables have a separate initial operation boundary: arithmetic/exp, broadcasting, declared-node/counter selection and explicit reductions. Their required tests check independent nonuniform-grid values, JAX float64 JIT/vmap and state/parameter/time derivatives, and Torch float64/float32 autograd. Static measure/coordinate metadata is outside that derivative contract. Broader RHS qualification does not automatically qualify additional observable operations or devices.

GPU execution is outside the qualified CPU matrix. The matrix describes the tested workload and paths, not every combination of compiler operators, backend versions, devices, or automatic differentiation transforms.

docs.title: Independent equations and structural checks
docs.text:
benchmarks/hierarchical_model.py defines a synthetic closed three-compartment relaxation network. State and a local rate vary by group, while a global gain, stage recovery rates, and a stage transport matrix are shared. Aliases, stage reductions, and an apply_along transport expression exercise axis reordering and broadcasting. The reference uses explicit cell loops, not generated code or expressions copied from the compiler IR.

The coupled variant uses other groups' state through a group reduction. It matches the same independently written equations, and an attempted factorize_axes: [group] fails. Native block mapping is tested only for the independent variant, slicing local parameters while sharing global ones.

Transport is part of this fixture's equations. Operator descriptors intended for a downstream integration engine are a separate interface; compilation does not automatically apply every metadata operator to an RHS.

JAX checks JIT, batch evaluation, and shared/local parameter directional derivatives against finite differences of the independent reference. Torch checks autograd through state and shared/local parameters, with a reference finite-difference check. A closed RHS has conserved totals, so a squared-RHS objective is used to avoid an identically zero gradient from summing all flows.

docs.title: Local commands
docs.text:
From a clean checkout with uv and just installed:

just qualify-numpy
just qualify-jax
just qualify-torch
# Or run all three required core qualifications:
just qualify

The Torch target installs CPU wheels explicitly. These commands change the selected extras in the local environment; use separate worktrees/environments when retaining multiple dependency selections matters. They run the same qualification runner as CI. Normal quality, documentation, baseline tests, provider checks, and wheel validation remain required alongside qualification.

Scientific validity, agreement across untested parameter regimes, and solution accuracy of a downstream ODE/PDE integrator require separate evidence.

Literal RHS values, including zero and aliased constants, inherit the qualified floating state's precision during assembly. Flat, structured, and available block evaluation preserve dtype and namespace. Explicitly typed array-valued parameters retain their own precision; this rule does not coerce deliberately mixed-precision input arrays into the state dtype. Constant forcing has a zero state Jacobian under the tested JAX and Torch functional AD transforms.

Continuous-axis reduction weights use the floating state's dtype and device, including nested categorical sums and multi-axis trapezoidal integration. Analytic bilinear integrals on nonuniform grids qualify values, precision, namespace on all three CPU namespaces, JAX JIT, and JAX/Torch derivatives. Explicitly typed input arrays still follow native promotion; mixed-precision inputs remain unqualified.

Required compiler qualification also checks conditional scalar reaction balance artifacts against independent source-flux equations on NumPy, JAX and CPU Torch in float32/float64. The producer emits static exact integer weights and metadata; these tests qualify agreement with the represented native RHS, without claiming runtime integration accuracy, general stoichiometric inference or spatial and operator conservation. See reaction balances.

docs.title: Independent batches and normalization cost
docs.text:
Reaction callbacks enforce the declared template_shapes: a scalar state expects shape (), and an undeclared leading batch dimension raises an error with the reaction, state name, expected shape and received shape. Declare a categorical replicate axis for batched reactions. Passing arrays to a scalar specification does not implicitly add an independent replicate dimension.

For independent-clock stochastic engines, each reaction publishes independent_axes: declared factorize axes checked against that reaction's own propensity and coordinate mapping, before deterministic cancellation. An engine must also verify that all evolving state templates carry its chosen replicate axis and that no dynamics are omitted by reaction gaps or operators.

resolved_propensity_fn accepts current-time parameter slices in place of full time tables. Its time_varying_params lists consumed table names and full axes, so a consumer can select a different previous-table row for every replicate. This callback performs no interpolation or cache lookup. The ordinary propensity_fn still accepts full tables and scalar time. uses_time identifies explicit continuous-time dependence; declared table knots alone do not make such a propensity suitable for frozen-rate exact SSA.

A categorical axis can index independent parameter draws as well as model groups. Normalization expands the declared state cells and resolves their equations and parameter coordinates; it occurs before numerical evaluation or backend JIT compilation. The compiler caches lookup maps across these cells, so state membership, template selection, and coordinate lookup no longer repeat a scan over the entire axis for each reference.

For large independent batches, another useful option is to compile one block and map it over the batch. Declare factorize_axes only when no equation reduces, shifts, or mixes across the proposed batch axis. The compiler checks this condition and exposes block_pytree_eval_fn with that axis removed. Slice group-local parameters along with the state, and share global parameters:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from op_system import compile_spec

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "axes": [{"name": "draw", "coords": ["first", "second"]}],
    "factorize_axes": ["draw"],
    "state": ["X[draw]"],
    "equations": {"X[draw]": "-shared * rate[draw] * X[draw]"},
})
block = compiled.block_pytree_eval_fn
assert block is not None


def evaluate_one(x, rate):
    return block(0.0, {"X": x}, shared=0.5, rate=rate)["X"]


values = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
rates = jnp.array([0.2, 0.3, 0.4])
derivatives = jax.jit(jax.vmap(evaluate_one))(values, rates)

The numerical batch can have more draws than the small compilation fixture: the block evaluator contains no draw dimension. JAX mapping requires array parameters whose mapped dimensions match the state. CPU Torch can use the same pattern through torch.func.vmap, with Torch tensors and array operations. Qualify the operations in the particular model before assuming additional compiler or GPU support.

Mapping blocks changes compilation and evaluation costs, and does not speed up every workload. An equation such as sum_over(X[draw:d], draw=d) couples the draws and requires the monolithic evaluator. Removing that coupling to obtain a block evaluator would change the model.

Local rate aliases retain the same equations in full and block evaluation. For example, foi[loc] = beta * r0_loc[loc] * I[loc] uses a shared beta and a group-local r0_loc. Supply the selected local rate with the corresponding single-group state; expression and transition specifications should produce the same cell flows. Required CPU qualification checks this behavior in float32 and float64, including JAX compilation of the stripped evaluator.

docs.title: Capabilities and executable examples
docs.text: op_system compiles model definitions. An engine advances state and a provider adapts a framework's lifecycle. The MIT core does not import flepimop2; the separate GPL flepimop2-op_system distribution shares its release version.

docs.title: Model classes and numerical representations
docs.text:
Model class Specification/compiled contract Numerical consumer owns Spatial or trait-structured PDEs Continuous axes, shaped fields and transport/diffusion operator metadata Geometry, boundary treatment, discretization and integration Nonlocal / integro-differential dynamics Kernel reductions and conservative jump-integral contracts Kernel values, quadrature/discretization and operator staging ODEs and compartmental flows Expression equations or named transitions and flat/PyTree evaluators Time integration and accuracy policy Stochastic reaction networks Named reaction channels, propensities, dependencies and reported gaps Event/leap method, complete dynamics coverage and random streams

A PDE field represented on a numerical grid becomes a finite array. That array representation retains spatial/trait coordinates, measures, kernels and operator semantics; a right-hand-side callable is one part of the compiled contract. The SEIR and transfer examples below introduce model authoring. The operator guide covers spatial and nonlocal terms.

docs.title: Choose a public interface
docs.text:
Task Implemented interface Example and boundary Check or compile a specification validate_spec, normalize_rhs, compile_spec, compile_rhs Getting started: expression and transition SEIR; validation is structural, not proof of scientific correctness. Evaluate flat or structured state CompiledRhs.eval_fn, pytree_eval_fn State representations; use declared template shapes and state order. Evaluate independent blocks factorize_axes, block_pytree_eval_fn Independent batches; reductions or mixing across a proposed block axis invalidate independence. Export stochastic channels CompiledRhs.reactions, reaction_gaps, CompiledReaction Named transitions, reactants/dependencies and declared state shapes; a stochastic consumer must reject omitted dynamics. Resolve forcing once resolved_propensity_fn, time_varying_params, uses_time, independent_axes Time tables and batches; the consumer supplies correctly sliced parameters. Compute named latent quantities CompiledRhs.observables, CompiledObservable Latent observables: coordinates, reductions and physical measures; observation noise belongs downstream. Integrate selected positive states in log coordinates CompiledRhs.coordinate_view(), StateCoordinateView Log state coordinates; deterministic expressions and transitions with explicit encoding/decoding and domain flags. Inspect and fix shared scaling freedoms CompiledRhs.gauges, gauge_fix Scaling gauges; finite covariance probes and conservative homogeneity detection are not structural identifiability proofs. Inspect conditional conservation reaction_balances Reaction balances; respect reported gaps, parameter/sign assumptions and representation. Check independently specified equations qualify_rhs, QualificationFixture, QualificationConfig Numerical qualification; parity and invariant evidence is limited to the supplied fixtures. Supply spatial/operator metadata OperatorDescriptor, axis measures, kernels Operators; discretization and solving belong to a numerical engine.

NumPy, JAX and CPU Torch have a required qualification matrix. Array namespace selection happens at evaluation time. GPU execution and other Array API implementations need separate qualification for the intended model. convolve_history has a provider hook; history and delay remain reserved, unsupported operators. Metadata does not certify positivity or a physical model.

docs.title: Run the combined compiler example
docs.text:
From a source checkout:

uv sync --dev
just example-reactions
just doctest

examples/independent_reactions.py validates a two-replicate transfer model, compiles a held rate table and evaluates a named population observable. The independently known derivatives are [0, -10, 0, 10] before the forcing change and [-2, -2, 2, 2] at it; each replicate keeps its own population, 10 or 20. This evaluates the compiler; op_engine provides independent-clock SSA.

docs.title: Read the compiled output
docs.text:
Evaluation Replicate dS/dt dI/dt Population t = 0.5 a 0 0 10 t = 0.5 b -10 10 20 t = 1 a -2 2 10 t = 1 b -2 2 20

The state stays fixed at S = [10, 20], I = [0, 0] in both evaluations. The bars compare compiled propensities at two times. At t = 1, the right-continuous table selects its new row. Each transfer has opposite drift contributions to S and I, preserving its own population. No integration is performed in this compiler example.

Download the vector PDF. Regenerate the figure and table from the actual checked example:

uv run --with matplotlib==3.11.2 python examples/illustrate_reactions.py
just figures-check

Matplotlib is needed only for regeneration. The check reruns the compiler fixture, compares the table and full plotted data, and verifies source/export fingerprints. The docs build runs that check and includes the generated table directly. The plotted data records the numerical inputs.

A scalar template has shape (). To evaluate replicated reactions, declare a replicate axis in the specification. A leading dimension on scalar state does not create one. Held tables are right-continuous; exact frozen-rate SSA also requires no continuous time dependence between changes.

docs.title: What runs automatically
docs.text:
just doctest runs public API examples and the actual README/SEIR guide code, including the standalone example. just ci includes those tests plus the broader core/provider suite, strict typing, lint and documentation checks. Public docstrings cover compilation, reaction shape metadata, balances and independent-equation qualification. They use small deterministic results; backend differentiation and broader conformance remain in dedicated tests.

When changing an API or example, update its guide and docstring together. Keep complete workflows executable, assert an independent equation or invariant, and run the real documentation text rather than a copied test-only version. Run just qualify and just build-all before a PR as described in Contributing.

docs.title: Expression selectors and reduction bindings
docs.text:
Within an expression, X[loc, age:ap] keeps the current loc selection while binding the age position to the reduction variable ap. For example:

total[loc] = apply_along(X[loc, age:ap], age=ap, kernel=sum)

loc comes from the alias's left-hand side; ap visits the declared age coordinates. Nested reductions can bind additional axes without dropping the unreduced group selector. The resulting total stays local to each group, so a group block evaluator can retain its independence.

Use axis:variable inside expression brackets and axis=variable in the reducer's keyword arguments. Historical examples that put axis=variable inside a state subscript are not valid expression syntax in the typed-IR compiler. Rewrite them using colon selectors and an expression-first reducer call as above. Invalid alias expressions fail with the alias's context instead of becoming partially expanded state names.

Initial-state parameter names and expanded transition labels retain a separate compatibility string-substitution path. When that path binds a wildcard in a mixed selector, it preserves all explicitly bound entries; it must not collapse the whole selector into a cell name containing only the wildcard axis. This compatibility behavior does not make equals selectors valid expression syntax.

docs.title: Writing a compartmental model
docs.text:
This SEIR example introduces the syntax through one deterministic compartmental model. The same specification layer also describes spatial/trait fields, nonlocal kernel interactions and stochastic channels. See the model-class map and operator contracts for the corresponding interfaces and boundaries.

Install the core compiler and a YAML reader:

python -m pip install op-system PyYAML

The compiler accepts a Python mapping. YAML/JSON loading is a caller concern; compile_spec(spec) validates, normalizes, and compiles it. normalize_rhs(spec) returns a normalized model without compilation, and validate_spec(spec) returns a structural report. There is no public load_spec file loader.

Optional parameter declarations attach support, units, descriptions and fixed/free status to inferred RHS parameters for downstream consumers, without changing numerical evaluation.

docs.title: A complete age-structured SEIR model
docs.text:
Save the following as examples/age-seir.yaml (create the examples directory first), or use the checked example. The groups are categorical population bins, so mixing uses an unweighted sum. Rates are per unit time. This synthetic example demonstrates authoring and balance checks; choose and independently qualify your scientific equations.

# Shared rate beta; susceptibility varies by target age group.
kind: transitions
axes:
  - name: age
    type: categorical
    coords: [young, old]
state: ["S[age]", "E[age]", "I[age]", "R[age]"]
aliases:
  "N[age]": "S[age] + E[age] + I[age] + R[age]"
  "foi[age]": "beta * susceptibility[age] * apply_along(C[age:s,age] * I[age:s] / N[age:s], age=s, kernel=sum)"
transitions:
  - name: infection
    from: "S[age]"
    to: "E[age]"
    rate: "foi[age]"
  - name: progression
    from: "E[age]"
    to: "I[age]"
    rate: "kappa"
  - name: recovery
    from: "I[age]"
    to: "R[age]"
    rate: "gamma"
# Optional provider seed metadata; runtime values are supplied separately.
initial_state:
  "S[age]": {shaped: S0, axes: [age]}
  "E[age]": {shaped: E0, axes: [age]}
  "I[age]": {shaped: I0, axes: [age]}
  "R[age]": {shaped: R0, axes: [age]}

state order fixes the flat layout: all young/old S cells, then E, I, and R. Each bracketed state carries only its listed axes. Bare states are scalar; there is no automatic inheritance of every declared axis. Quote selectors in YAML flow lists, because their brackets and commas are part of the string.

An alias is an expression, not another compartment. N[age] is the current population in that age bin. C[source_age, target_age] has source rows and target columns: C[age:s,age] binds the first index to source s, keeps the second at the current target age, and sums the source prevalence I/N. Use an asymmetric matrix while checking orientation; a symmetric matrix can hide a transpose.

A transition with from uses a per-capita hazard: the infection flow is foi[age] * S[age], not just foi[age]. Do not multiply by the source a second time in its rate. from omitted/null creates an absolute source inflow. to must name a declared state: omitted/null sink destinations are currently unsupported and fail validation. Use an expression equation for an open loss, or track the loss in an explicit compartment. The latter retains the lost amount in the declared state total and exports a closed transfer reaction. A closed transition subtracts and adds the same flow, preserving population.

These standalone alternatives both give x' = -k*x; the explicit loss compartment additionally gives loss' = k*x:

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec

open_loss = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "state": ["x"],
    "equations": {"x": "-k*x"},
})
tracked_loss = compile_spec({
    "kind": "transitions",
    "state": ["x", "loss"],
    "transitions": [{"name": "loss", "from": "x", "to": "loss", "rate": "k"}],
})
open_derivative = open_loss.eval_fn(0.0, np.asarray([3.0]), k=2.0)  # [-6]
tracked_derivative = tracked_loss.eval_fn(0.0, np.asarray([3.0, 0.0]), k=2.0)  # [-6, 6]

Expression equations do not currently export executable jump reactions; choose the representation required by the consuming deterministic/stochastic engine.

initial_state records provider seed parameter names and constants. It does not allocate or initialize core arrays. A consuming framework resolves S0, E0, I0, and R0; core callers supply the state themselves as below. The shaped form states the parameter's axis order explicitly. A scalar mapping such as S: S0 or a per-cell template such as "S[age]": "S0[age]" is also supported.

A state that starts at a known constant (typically 0 for a cumulative counter fed by a source-only transition) needs no seed parameter: give the key a numeric literal, for example "C[age]": 0.0 or D: 0. The literal is broadcast to every cell the key selects (a pinned coordinate such as "C[age=young]": 0.0 selects one), is stored as a float in compiled.meta["initial_state"], and requests no provider parameter. It must be a finite real number; booleans, nan, and inf are rejected. There is no {fixed: ...}/{value: ...} mapping spelling, and a quoted "0.0" is still a parameter name. States omitted from initial_state are left to the consuming framework (the op_engine provider uses zero, but a literal records the intent explicitly).

docs.title: Evaluate the example
docs.text:
Run from the directory containing examples/age-seir.yaml. The scalar parameters beta, kappa, and gamma are shared, susceptibility varies over the target age axis, and C is shared as a two-axis matrix. Arrays use float64 throughout. compiled.param_names lists inputs; validate_spec(spec).parameters reports scalar and shaped parameter axes; compiled.template_shapes describes the structured layout.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import yaml

from op_system import compile_spec

spec = yaml.safe_load(Path("examples/age-seir.yaml").read_text())
compiled = compile_spec(spec)
state = {
    "S": np.asarray([900.0, 600.0]),
    "E": np.asarray([20.0, 10.0]),
    "I": np.asarray([30.0, 40.0]),
    "R": np.asarray([50.0, 50.0]),
}
params = {
    "beta": 0.3,
    "kappa": 0.2,
    "gamma": 0.1,
    "susceptibility": np.asarray([1.0, 0.7]),
    "C": np.asarray([[4.0, 1.0], [2.0, 3.0]]),
}
flat = np.concatenate([state[name] for name in ("S", "E", "I", "R")])
flat_rhs = compiled.eval_fn(0.0, flat, **params)
assert compiled.pytree_eval_fn is not None
rhs = compiled.pytree_eval_fn(0.0, state, **params)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    flat_rhs, np.concatenate([rhs[name] for name in ("S", "E", "I", "R")])
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(sum(rhs.values()), np.zeros(2), atol=1e-12)
print(np.round(np.stack(list(rhs.values())), 3))

Expected rows are S, E, I, R, with columns young, old:

[[-63.257 -25.38 ]
 [ 59.257  23.38 ]
 [  1.     -2.   ]
 [  3.      4.   ]]

This evaluates a derivative. Use a numerical engine to integrate it in time. For scientific checks beyond structural validation, use qualify_rhs with independently written equations and fixtures. The guide's CI test executes these exact YAML/Python fences and checks cell flows and per-age conservation against an independent loop oracle.

docs.title: Equations and expression syntax
docs.text:
Use kind: expr with one equation for each declared state to write derivatives directly. The following equations are equivalent to the transitions above when the same axes, aliases, and state are retained and transitions is removed:

kind: expr
equations:
  "S[age]": "-foi[age] * S[age]"
  "E[age]": "foi[age] * S[age] - kappa * E[age]"
  "I[age]": "kappa * E[age] - gamma * I[age]"
  "R[age]": "gamma * I[age]"

Expressions support allowlisted arithmetic, named state/parameter references, aliases, and documented helper calls. They are not arbitrary Python programs: imports, attribute traversal, and arbitrary function calls are rejected. Reference a templated state as I[age]; a bare I is invalid unless a scalar state I is declared. Expression bindings use age:s inside brackets and age=s in reducer arguments. Endpoint pinning uses "S[age=young]" in transition selectors. See expression selectors, global totals, and aging chains.

docs.title: Axes and mixing choices
docs.text:
Axis type Coordinates and reduction Categorical (default) Unique nonempty labels; sum_over / apply_along(..., kernel=sum) use unweighted sums Ordinal Unique labels in declared order; reductions use sums while directional operators use the order Continuous Strictly increasing numeric coordinates; integrate_over / default apply_along use trapezoidal weights, requiring at least two points except the special constant time-table axis

Nonuniform continuous grids carry quadrature weights; interpreting population counts as density values changes units. sum_state() totals declared cells without quadrature. For example, sum_over(I[age:a], age=a) sums discrete age bins, while integrate_over(u[x:i], x=i) integrates a field over continuous x. Time is a separate forcing axis; see time-indexed parameters.

Add spatial/risk axes explicitly to states and use local parameters such as beta[loc]. An independent loc can be declared in factorize_axes: [loc] only when no RHS, alias, or operator couples locations. The compiler rejects invalid factorization; see independent batches. Full and block layouts are separate choices from the runtime array namespace.

Core callers supply matrix C as a parameter. Provider users can alternatively declare kernels with an explicit value matrix or a supported analytic form and declared numeric axes; the provider constructs and injects those values. Core compilation preserves these declarations as metadata and does not itself materialize analytic kernels. See the provider README and coverage audit for generation contracts.

docs.title: Operators and splitting
docs.text: An operators block describes processes for a consuming numerical engine, separately from equations/transitions. For example, an ordinal immune-state axis can declare advection with a rate parameter and direction, while a continuous trait can declare conservative jumps. Compilation exposes typed descriptors in compiled.operators; eval_fn alone does not advance or apply these metadata operators. The engine must resolve coefficients, discretization, boundaries, and splitting stages. Follow the operator guide for supported schemas and conservative reference functions; do not count a process twice by also including it in the RHS.

docs.title: Cross-axis constraints: current boundary
docs.text:
constraints is currently a reserved metadata block. Public normalization preserves it verbatim; the private constraint parser's validation does not provide public masking. State expansion and reductions still cover the full Cartesian product. Filtering and constraint-aware reductions are not implemented.

The planned schema uses at least two axes and either allow or exclude:

# Planned masking metadata; this does not remove current compartments.
constraints:
  - axes: [age, vax]
    allow:
      - {age: young, vax: [none]}
      - {age: old}

An allow rule would retain its matching combinations; an omitted axis in a rule would match all its coordinates. An exclude rule would remove matches. Until filtering is implemented, represent asymmetric populations explicitly, for example state: ["S_young", "S_old[vax]"], with equations/transitions for those states and independently checked totals. Do not rely on this reserved block to prevent invalid flows or omit state cells.

docs.title: Global state totals
docs.text:
sum_state() sums every element of every declared state buffer, including scalar compartments and stages generated by chain. Aliases, parameters, synthetic operator constants, and extra keys supplied to a structured evaluator are not additional states. The result is an unweighted sum; continuous-axis quadrature remains an explicit modeling choice through the integration helpers.

Optional state representations and physical measures describe extensive counts/mass and intensive densities without changing this helper. A density's physical integral requires its declared measure; an unweighted density sum generally has a different meaning.

The helper works in expressions, aliases, transition rates, and exported reaction propensities on qualified CPU backends. Flat and structured evaluation use native array reductions, so JAX tracing and Torch parameter gradients retain the same calculation. Totals are cached within an evaluation and refreshed on the next call with its new state.

A global total across groups is a coupling dependency. The compiler rejects a factorize_axes declaration that would turn such a model into independent blocks. When the intended equations are local, write an explicitly local total, for example N[group] = sum_over(S[group,age:a] + I[group,age:a], age=a). Changing a global denominator to a local denominator changes the equations.

For a staged chain named I, declaring state: [S, R] lets the helper generate I1, I2, and so on. Declaring I as well creates an additional, separate compartment, and its value contributes to sum_state() even if its derivative is zero. The chain prefix alone is not a compartment declaration.

Reaction export preserves numerical propensity evaluation. A population-normalized rate need not have a polynomial mass-action description or a certified elasticity bound. Follow the chosen engine's metadata requirements and the documented reactants: auto restrictions independently of whether export succeeds.

docs.title: Hierarchical compiler benchmarks
docs.text:
The synthetic workload in benchmarks/hierarchical_model.py describes three nonlinear relaxation compartments over group and stage axes. Its aliases, sum_over reducers, and apply_along stage transport preserve readable model structure. One shared gain and transport matrix coexist with group-local rates and initial conditions. Increasing groups grows local parameters and states; increasing stages also grows the shared kernel quadratically.

The independent variant declares factorize_axes: [group]. The coupled variant uses the mean of a state across groups and omits that declaration. It has no block result: treating its groups as independent would change the equations. Required qualification tests also reject a forced independence declaration for that coupled model.

docs.title: Reproduce a run
docs.text:
Use a supported Python version, sync the checkout, and install desired backends. These commands select CPU Torch and enable JAX's double precision inside each worker. NumPy alone is enough for the default benchmark command.

uv sync --dev --extra jax
uv pip install 'torch>=2.6' --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
just benchmark --backends numpy jax torch --groups 4 16 --stages 2 4 \
  --coupling both --dtype float64 --repeats 5 --inner-loops 100 \
  --warmups 3 --output benchmark.json

Repeat with --dtype float32 to qualify that precision separately. For a quick correctness-only sweep, add --check-only. just qualify executes small correctness cases in the required NumPy/JAX/Torch jobs and rejects skipped backend cases. Larger timing runs remain opt-in; CI has no wall-time thresholds. The runner aborts if a requested backend is missing or a case fails agreement.

Each case runs serially in a fresh process. Workers request one thread through OMP_NUM_THREADS, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, and MKL_NUM_THREADS; JAX uses CPU. These settings do not pin CPU affinity or guarantee that every runtime uses exactly one thread. Keep other heavy workloads idle when collecting evidence. The command is also available as uv run --no-sync python -m scripts.benchmark_hierarchical with the same arguments.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
Every generated and handwritten layout must first agree with independent cell-wise NumPy equations. Checks cover shape, dtype, namespace, and RHS values. JAX and Torch also compare the derivative of the squared RHS norm with respect to the shared gain against central differences of the independent equations. NumPy records that AD comparison as unavailable. The reference finite-difference step, tolerances, values, and errors are retained in the result. This checks one fixture and one parameter direction, not all derivatives or scientific regimes.

Result Meaning normalize Specification validation, alias/template processing, and normalized IR construction compile_rhs Compilation from already normalized IR, including lowering and generated Python callables backend_setup_seconds Backend import and conversion of the resident input arrays cold_jit_seconds JAX tracing/lowering/native compilation of a new evaluator wrapper; null for NumPy and eager Torch first_evaluation_seconds First synchronized call after that explicit JAX compilation, or after eager correctness checks warm Samples of average synchronized RHS latency, with median, minimum, and maximum warm_calls_per_second Reciprocal of median warm latency fixture_bytes Host state/parameter array payload, excluding Python objects and runtimes process_peak_rss_bytes Worker peak resident memory on Linux/macOS, including imports, correctness/AD checks, and every layout

Normalization and compiler samples repeat independently of warm evaluation. Each warm sample averages inner_loops calls after warmups calls. JAX outputs are synchronized on every call. Inputs are already resident; device transfers, ODE integration, and likelihood calculations are outside the measurement. Correctness runs before explicit JIT timings, so this is function compilation cost in an initialized backend, not whole-process startup. Shapes are fixed per case. No Torch compilation or GPU timing claim is made.

All layouts accept the same structured input and return structured derivatives. The flat wrapper includes packing/unpacking. NumPy block evaluation uses a Python loop; JAX and Torch use native vmap. These different execution policies are part of the recorded layout comparison, not interchangeable timing paths. The handwritten vectorized implementation uses a matrix multiply for transport; the independent oracle uses cell loops and is never timed as the handwritten implementation.

JSON includes the fixture definition, dimensions, specification size, array payload, full samples, repeat policy, dtype, Python/compiler/backend versions, CPU/platform information, thread settings, command arguments, and source commit with dirty-checkout status. Keep the JSON with any published timing claim. Peak RSS is a process high-water mark, not an incremental tensor or per-layout memory measurement. JAX workers may use more threads than the requested BLAS policy.

docs.title: Interpreting the tradeoff
docs.text:
The structured specification supplies named compartments, alias relationships, parameter locality, and independence metadata from one model description. Generated code avoids maintaining separate backend equations. That authoring benefit carries normalization/code-generation overhead and does not imply a universal speedup over well-written native code.

A preliminary serial CPU sweep at 4 and 16 groups with 3 stages, float64, Python 3.13.13, NumPy 2.5.4, JAX 0.11.2, and CPU Torch 2.14.1 used an Intel Core Ultra 7 265U, three repeats of 30 calls after three warmups. All 12 independent/coupled backend cases agreed with their references. Handwritten NumPy was faster than generated evaluation in those cases; NumPy's Python block loop grew with group count. JAX layouts were often close at these small shapes, while eager Torch results varied substantially.
