This small sweep motivates larger, repeated measurements rather than a ranking or performance threshold.

docs.title: Related tools and a fair comparison
docs.text:
Other tools already connect model authoring to execution. The pyodesys project offers symbolic ODE systems, automatic Jacobians, native code generation, and integration interfaces; see its software paper. MCSimMod wraps GNU MCSim models for use with R's deSolve and native C compilation; see its software paper.

Tool Authoring/execution focus relevant to this workload op_system Restricted specifications, explicit axes/aliases/operators, runtime array namespace, structured/block RHS metadata pyodesys Symbolic/numerical ODE definitions, Jacobians and integration, including native code-generation options MCSimMod MCSim model files, R/deSolve integration, native C model execution

This runner measures only op_system and handwritten native functions. It does not report cross-tool timings. A fair future comparison must implement identical equations, fixtures, precision, and coupling; verify values first; and separate model preprocessing, native compilation, and warm RHS evaluation. Compare integration only with matching solvers, tolerances, output points, and error criteria. Report unavailable AD/block features explicitly rather than assigning them artificial timings. The tools' authoring and integration scope should accompany any speed comparison.

docs.title: Named latent observables
docs.text:
Optional observables define instantaneous quantities separately from the RHS. They work with expression and transition models. CompiledRhs.observables is a read-only mapping of names to CompiledObservable records. Each contains a definition, concrete output shape and coordinate labels, direct state and parameter dependencies, explicit time use, applied physical measures, and native flat/PyTree evaluators. Records and evaluator protocols are also exported from op_system.observables and the package root.

kind: expr
axes:
  - name: x
    type: continuous
    coords: [0.05, 0.25, 0.7]
    measure: {kind: cell, weights: [0.1, 0.3, 0.6], units: m}
state: ["rho[x]", "mass[x]", counter]
equations:
  rho[x]: "0"
  mass[x]: "0"
  counter: "-k*counter"
state_metadata:
  rho: {representation: density, units: items/m, measure_axes: [x]}
  mass: {representation: cell_mass, measure_axes: []}
  counter: {representation: cumulative}
parameters:
  gain: {support: positive}
observables:
  physical_total:
    expr: "gain*rho[x]"
    reduction: {kind: integral, axes: [x]}
    units: items
  extensive_total:
    expr: "mass[x]"
    reduction: {kind: sum, axes: [x]}
  counter_value:
    expr: counter
  center_sample:
    expr: "rho[0.25]"
  field:
    expr: "gain*rho[x]"
    axes: [x]

The counter equation here illustrates that its representation annotation does not establish monotonicity. Choose the scientific counter dynamics explicitly.

Definitions require expr. Optional axes give output axes after reduction; omission means scalar output. Optional reduction has exactly kind (sum or integral) and a nonempty, unique list of axes. Output and reduction axes must be disjoint and declared by the model. units and description are optional nonempty strings. Unknown fields, unresolved axes/coordinates and incompatible parameter layouts fail before returning a compiled artifact. An empty mapping or omitted observables leaves the existing RHS interface unchanged.

The initial pointwise subset is +, -, *, /, **, unary +/-, and unary np.exp. State arrays require named subscripts, such as rho[x]; scalar states use bare names. A literal coordinate selects an existing declared node, such as rho[0.25]. Named categorical selection also works, such as rho[region:left,x]. This selection does not interpolate. Bare nonstate symbols are inferred as scalar parameters; subscripted nonstate symbols define shaped parameter buffers. Shaped parameters use complete arrays under their base names and must have exactly their exported shapes. Expanded scalar parameter keywords are not an observation-buffer interface.

sum applies unit weights even on continuous axes. integral uses only the explicit axis measure from state representations, once per reduced axis. Intensive state dependencies must declare density or concentration and measure_axes; extensive counts, cell masses and cumulative counters reject physical weighting. Partial spatial integration retains output axes while applying only the requested measures. Multiple physical axes use separable products of the declared weights. Extra noncounting measure axes must be required by at least one referenced intensive state. Parameter-only constant integrands are allowed with explicitly declared measures.

These checks distinguish known extensive states and physical measures. They do not establish dimensions, geometry, or the units of arbitrary products and parameter fields; supplied output units remain annotations. Legacy equation reducers and their continuous-axis deltas are unchanged. Nested reducers, aliases, observer-to-observer references, history, time-varying parameter buffers, partial/duplicate state-base layouts, and other pointwise functions are outside this first subset and fail explicitly.

For the example, rho(x)=1+2*x has exact cell-average values [1.1,1.5,2.4]. Declared widths give integral 2, while the unweighted density sum is 5. The extensive masses [0.11,0.45,1.44] sum directly to 2.

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec

compiled = compile_spec({
    "state": ["x"],
    "equations": {"x": "-k*x"},
    "parameters": {"gain": {"support": "positive"}},
    "observables": {"scaled": {"expr": "gain*x+t", "units": "declared-output"}},
})
y = np.array([2.0])
rhs_value = compiled.eval_fn(3.0, y, k=0.5)  # gain is not an RHS requirement
observable = compiled.observables["scaled"]
observed = observable.eval_fn(3.0, y, gain=4.0)  # scalar native value: 11
assert np.asarray(observed).shape == observable.output_shape == ()
assert observable.parameter_shapes == (("gain", ()),)

Observable-only parameter declarations are accepted in parameters, without adding them to the RHS param_names or equation binding requirements. validate_spec's consumed parameter report continues to describe dynamics; observable requirements are exported independently in parameter_shapes. State/parameter dependencies describe the instantaneous expression, not all indirect solution sensitivities. time_dependent specifically indicates an explicit t reference; a state-dependent observable can evolve in time even without one.

eval_fn(t,y,**params) consumes the complete flat (len(state_names),) state. pytree_eval_fn consumes all state bases with their natural shapes, including zero-dimensional scalar arrays. States must share a namespace and real floating dtype. Array parameters must use that namespace; host scalar/list constants are converted and native arrays are cast without detaching derivatives. Results use the state dtype and declared shape. Evaluators perform functional operations and may return views, so treat inputs and outputs as immutable. Trusted model pickle round trips rebuild these evaluators with their detached definitions.

The required qualification runner includes independent nonuniform-grid values, axis reordering, shaped parameters, counters and declared-node samples. NumPy checks analytic values; JAX checks float64 JIT/vmap and state/parameter/time derivatives; CPU Torch checks those derivatives in float64 and float32. Gradient checks use the initial arithmetic/exp subset and static measures. They do not qualify mesh-coordinate/measure derivatives, Torch compiler transforms, GPUs, discontinuities or generic future operations.

Numerical interpolation, time windows and integrals, trajectory storage and mesh transfer belong to consuming engines. Noise, censoring and missingness belong to statistical measurement models. Global observations stay on the full compiled model even when dynamics have a per-block evaluator; summing independent dynamic blocks can still couple a statistical objective.

Point quadrature integrates point samples over their coordinate span, whereas cell measures apply the discretization owner's widths/volumes to cell averages. For the point-rule reference see SciPy trapezoid. The compiler evaluates the supplied measures with native products and reductions so it does not introduce a SciPy runtime or assume a geometry from cell centers.

docs.title: Log state coordinates
docs.text:
Available in OP System 0.9.0. This feature applies to deterministic expression and transition RHS evaluation, including supported named fields and nonlocal expression reductions.

Declare state_metadata: {x: {scale: log}} to request z = log(x) for every expanded component of state base x. Other states use identity coordinates. Model expressions, initial physical values and observable expressions continue to describe physical quantities. Build an explicit model.coordinate_view() once, outside the solver callback. The original compiled model remains in its natural coordinates.

StateDeclaration.scale defaults to identity. The record now has five fields; existing four-argument construction remains valid, but code unpacking four tuple items needs to use named attributes or include the new field.

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec

model = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "state": ["x", "collected"],
    "state_metadata": {"x": {"scale": "log"}},
    "equations": {"x": "-rate*x", "collected": "rate*x"},
    "observables": {"total": {"expr": "x+collected"}},
})
view = model.coordinate_view()
z0 = view.encode(np.array([1.0, 0.0]))
rhs = view.bind({"rate": 2.0})
np.testing.assert_allclose(rhs(0, z0), [-2.0, 2.0])
np.testing.assert_allclose(view.observables["total"].eval_fn(0, z0), 1.0)

The flat callback takes (n_state,) arrays. Adapt that layout to the solver's state layout explicitly. The flepimop2 providers do not automatically select the coordinate view from metadata. Decode results before reporting physical trajectories or applying output-state diagnostics. For an (output_time, state, ...) array use view.decode_native(trajectory, state_axis=1) and inspect its valid flag. Initial-state expressions and provider initialization remain in natural units; encode the evaluated initial state explicitly. The view exposes shaped pytree_eval_fn and independent block_pytree_eval_fn when the source model supports them. Its PyTree encoders accept complete state dictionaries, including buffers with an independent block axis already stripped.

docs.title: OP Engine core example
docs.text:
OP Engine's ModelCore retains a subgroup axis, including for this single-group example. With OP System 0.9.0 and OP Engine 0.8.0, the following adapter connects the flat callback above to its deterministic CoreSolver interface:

from op_engine import CoreSolver, ModelCore

core = ModelCore(n_states=2, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 21))
core.set_initial_state(z0[:, None])


def engine_rhs(time, state):
    return rhs(time, state[:, 0])[:, None]


CoreSolver(core).run(engine_rhs)
decoded = view.decode_native(core.state_array, state_axis=1)
assert bool(decoded.valid)
assert decoded.state.shape == (21, 2, 1)
np.testing.assert_allclose(decoded.state[-1, 0, 0], np.exp(-2.0))

The callback removes the single subgroup axis before evaluating the compiled RHS and restores it on the derivative. This is an adapter for the example's layout; do not discard axes from a different model without matching its compiled state order and template shapes. The known exponential remaining-state value checks the coordinate/solver connection, not the accuracy of the collected state or its numerical total.

docs.title: Equation and domain
docs.text:
For a selected component, the view compiles F_i(x)/x_i and evaluates it at x = exp(z). It cancels syntactically exact multiplicative factors before division where supported. For dx/dt = -rate*x, this gives dz/dt = -rate even if exp(z) underflows. This simplification is not a general symbolic limit calculation: an additive source b-rate*x requires b/x-rate and can overflow when x is extremely small. Aliases, total-state helpers, time tables and observables receive decoded physical state.

view.encode rejects nonfinite state values and zero or negative selected components before evaluating logarithms. There is no implicit floor or clamp. Select log coordinates only for states whose intended deterministic trajectory stays strictly positive; a cumulative counter starting at zero usually needs identity coordinates. The metadata is a coordinate request, not a proof that the equations preserve positivity.

NumPy, JAX and CPU Torch transforms retain the source namespace and floating dtype. Use encode_native, decode_native, encode_pytree_native and decode_pytree_native inside JIT, vmap or automatic differentiation. They return CoordinateResult(state, valid) without extracting host scalars. Invalid native inputs can produce nonfinite outputs. Decoding can underflow to zero or overflow; the scalar native flag reports either failure, and decode_checked checks it eagerly. decode is the unchecked native value operation used in callbacks. Flags describe domain and representability, not solver accuracy. Signed identity states are masked before logarithms/exponentials so inactive branches do not contaminate derivatives.

docs.title: Numerical behavior and exported structure
docs.text:
The checked example uses a deliberately large Euler step for dx/dt = -2*x, d(collected)/dt = 2*x, starting at (1, 0). Its independently known solution at time one gives the following values.

Quantity at time one Direct Euler Log Euler, decoded Exact Remaining x -1.000000 0.135335 0.135335 Collected 2.000000 2.000000 0.864665 Total 1.000000 2.135335 1.000000

Log Euler is exact for this particular remaining-state equation. The collected state is inaccurate, and the decoded discrete total is not conserved. Smaller steps, error controls and independent solution checks still matter. A change of coordinates also changes the meaning of a solver's error norm and tolerances.

Natural-scale reaction balance laws remain applicable to the continuous physical equations after decoding. Their original linear coefficients do not become linear laws of log coordinates. The view therefore does not export reaction artifacts, balances or the source model's derivative and affinity metadata as coordinate-space claims. Obtain coordinate Jacobians by differentiating the view evaluator; nonlinear changes can alter sparsity and affine dependence. The retained view.natural model still exports its original artifacts. Stochastic SSA consumes those original physical states and integer jumps; the log view transforms deterministic drift only.

Separate operator descriptors and history callbacks require a transformed composition contract and currently reject log-view creation. This restriction does not exclude named-field or nonlocal dynamics already represented in the instantaneous expression RHS.

For gauge-fixed models, first encode original parameters and initial physical state with model.gauge_fix.encode. Then log-encode that representative with the coordinate view. To recover original units, decode log coordinates first and then apply the retained gauge inverse. Gauge anchors stay bound across coordinate RHS and observable callbacks.

docs.title: Named-axis kernel products
docs.text:
Two different axes can index a rectangular parameter table. For example, K[consumer,resource] has one row for each consumer and one column for each resource. State arrays need not have the same length. The named selectors identify which axis is summed, including when the matrix is used in the opposite direction.

Expression Independent array calculation apply_along(K[consumer,resource:r]*P[resource:r], resource=r, kernel=sum) K @ P apply_along(g[consumer:c]*K[consumer:c,resource]*Z[consumer:c], consumer=c, kernel=sum) K.T @ (g * Z)

The normalizer infers the parameter's axis order from its named references; validate_spec(spec).parameters reports the contract. Supply K with the reported shape and order. Distinct axis names make the intended row/column roles explicit, rather than relying on equal lengths to conceal a transpose.

The complete executable example includes both products and a per-coordinate choice of linear or quadratic loss:

"""Two distinct named axes, rectangular interactions and conditional losses.

Run ``uv run python examples/named_kernel_products.py``. All inputs are
synthetic. The independent reference uses ordinary matrix products.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec


def model_spec(resources: int = 3, consumers: int = 2) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Describe interaction between two differently sized groups of variables.

    Returns:
        A specification with resource and consumer axes and a rectangular table.
    """
    return {
        "kind": "expr",
        "axes": [
            {"name": "resource", "coords": [f"r{i}" for i in range(resources)]},
            {"name": "consumer", "coords": [f"c{i}" for i in range(consumers)]},
        ],
        "state": ["P[resource]", "Z[consumer]"],
        "aliases": {
            "exposure[consumer]": (
                "apply_along(K[consumer,resource:r]*P[resource:r], "
                "resource=r, kernel=sum)"
            ),
            "removal[resource]": (
                "apply_along(g[consumer:c]*K[consumer:c,resource]*Z[consumer:c], "
                "consumer=c, kernel=sum)"
            ),
        },
        "equations": {
            "P[resource]": "-P[resource]*removal[resource]",
            "Z[consumer]": (
                "efficiency[consumer]*Z[consumer]*exposure[consumer] - "
                "np.where(linear[consumer] > 0, loss[consumer]*Z[consumer], "
                "loss[consumer]*Z[consumer]*Z[consumer])"
            ),
        },
    }


def inputs(resources: int = 3, consumers: int = 2) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict[str, Any]]:
    """Return seeded states and a table ordered as consumer by resource."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(312)
    state = rng.uniform(0.3, 2.0, size=resources + consumers)
    params = {
        "K": rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, size=(consumers, resources)) / resources,
        "g": rng.uniform(0.2, 1.0, size=consumers),
        "efficiency": rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8, size=consumers),
        "loss": rng.uniform(0.05, 0.3, size=consumers),
        "linear": np.arange(consumers) % 2,
    }
    return state, params


def reference(state: np.ndarray, params: dict[str, Any]) -> np.ndarray:
    """Compute the same equations directly, without the specification compiler.

    Returns:
        Flat resource and consumer derivatives in declared state order.
    """
    consumers, resources = params["K"].shape
    p, z = state[:resources], state[resources : resources + consumers]
    resource_loss = -p * (params["K"].T @ (params["g"] * z))
    consumer_change = params["efficiency"] * z * (params["K"] @ p) - np.where(
        params["linear"] > 0, params["loss"] * z, params["loss"] * z**2
    )
    return np.concatenate([resource_loss, consumer_change])


def main() -> None:
    """Check the compiled equations against the independent rectangular product."""
    state, params = inputs()
    compiled = compile_spec(model_spec())
    result = compiled.eval_fn(0.0, state, **params)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(result, reference(state, params), rtol=1e-13, atol=1e-14)
    print(result)  # ruff: ignore[print] - command-line example output


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run uv run python examples/named_kernel_products.py. The example compares the compiled derivative with a separate NumPy implementation. Required backend qualification tests rectangular cases in NumPy, JAX and CPU PyTorch; JAX JIT and derivatives and PyTorch kernel gradients have independent checks.

docs.title: A fixed-state example
docs.text:
This synthetic example evaluates one state; it does not integrate a trajectory. Its binary-exact inputs are retained with the generated figure. The two consumer entries use different declared loss choices.

State Value Compiled derivative P[r0] 1 -0.265625 P[r1] 2 -0.6875 P[r2] 4 -2.25 Z[c0] 0.5 0.0625 Z[c1] 1.5 1.40625

Vector PDF · Inputs and outputs

docs.title: Conditional selection
docs.text:
np.where(condition, a, b) selects elementwise and dispatches through the state's array namespace. Conditions and branches can use shaped parameters, states and aliases. A condition such as linear[consumer] > 0 chooses the formula separately for each consumer.

Both branch expressions are evaluated. This is not lazy control flow: an inactive branch can still divide by zero, overflow or produce invalid gradients. Write expressions with valid numerical domains on both branches. Boolean parameters here choose between formulas; they do not create a stochastic event or change the reaction-network interpretation.

docs.title: Lowering and cost
docs.text:
For a single unweighted, unfiltered reduction over one axis and one free output axis, the compiler recognizes a two-axis matrix multiplied by a one-axis vector or vector product. It emits namespace-native matmul, avoiding the broadcast matrix-vector temporary. Named axes supply the transpose when needed. More general layouts, weighted quadrature, filtered sums and repeated physical-axis forms retain the general reduction path.

Vectorized flat and PyTree evaluators cache generated expression functions at compile time. Each call binds fresh state and parameter values; it does not invoke eval for each alias or equation. State/parameter shape checks and namespace discovery still have per-call costs. Scalar fallback evaluation is unchanged, and small problems can still spend more time in dispatch than in arithmetic. No runtime speed ratio is guaranteed.

An optional warmed NumPy comparison records compilation separately from evaluation and checks the independent equations before timing:

OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 uv run python -m \
  scripts.benchmark_named_kernels --sizes 4 16 128 256 512 1024

Large normalization cases can consume substantial time and memory. Start with the default smaller sweep when exploring a machine. These measurements are outside CI; CI checks numerical behavior and contraction structure without a wall-time threshold.

docs.title: Numerical qualification of compiled equations
docs.text: validate_spec checks structure, normalization, and compilation. Call qualify_rhs separately to compare the numerical RHS against equations you write independently. This is an opt-in, eager authoring tool: it evaluates named fixtures and returns inspectable host diagnostics. It does not add work to structural validation or to normal RHS evaluation.

docs.title: A first report
docs.text:
import json
import numpy as np
from op_system import QualificationFixture, compile_spec, qualify_rhs

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "axes": [{"name": "group", "coords": ["first", "second"]}],
    "factorize_axes": ["group"],
    "state": ["X[group]", "Y[group]"],
    "equations": {
        "X[group]": "-shared * local[group] * X[group]",
        "Y[group]": "shared * local[group] * X[group]",
    },
})


def reference(t, state, params):
    # A separate cell-wise calculation, not generated code or compiler IR.
    flux = np.empty_like(np.asarray(state["X"]))
    for group, x in enumerate(np.asarray(state["X"])):
        flux[group] = float(params["shared"]) * float(params["local"][group]) * x
    return {"X": -flux, "Y": flux}


fixtures = [
    QualificationFixture(
        "positive-closed",
        {"X": np.array([2.0, 3.0]), "Y": np.array([1.0, 0.5])},
        {"shared": 0.5, "local": np.array([0.2, 0.4])},
    )
]
report = qualify_rhs(
    compiled, fixtures, reference, evaluators=("flat", "structured", "block")
)
assert report.ok
print(json.dumps(report.to_dict(), indent=2, allow_nan=False))

Each fixture/layout record includes its name, time, array namespace, reference tolerances, shapes and dtypes, finite-value checks, and absolute/relative agreement errors. Failed numerical checks identify the state or callback. Exceptions raised by a user reference are reported against that fixture; other fixtures are still evaluated. JSON diagnostics use null for undefined or non-finite error metrics rather than invalid JSON numbers.

Fixtures use structured mappings keyed by compiled state templates, even for flat evaluation. Flat packing follows compiler metadata rather than fixture dictionary order. Scalar-only models can request evaluators=("flat",) when no structured evaluator is available.

docs.title: Conditional balance checks
docs.text:
Supply residual-to-zero callbacks through InvariantCheck. A conservation claim requires its conditions: the closed model above conserves each group's X + Y; external births, deaths, forcing, or sinks could invalidate that claim. The condition is recorded with the check and its absolute tolerance.

from op_system import InvariantCheck


def closed_balance(t, state, derivative, params):
    return derivative["X"] + derivative["Y"]


mass = InvariantCheck(
    "group total",
    closed_balance,
    "Closed X-to-Y transfer with no external sources",
    atol=1e-10,
)
balanced = qualify_rhs(compiled, fixtures, reference, invariants=(mass,))
assert balanced.ok

The utility checks the supplied residual; it cannot determine whether the condition accurately describes your model. An incorrect equation or violated balance produces a failed report. A coupled model that lacks a block evaluator produces an explicit failed block record, with no fallback to independent groups. Request only the evaluators applicable to that model.

docs.title: JAX state directions
docs.text:
Set a fixture's direction to a structured JAX state tangent to request an additional JAX JVP check against central differences of the independent reference. The state and tangent need matching keys, shapes, and compatible floating dtypes. The reference is called on eager perturbed states and may cross to NumPy. Qualification itself is not a function to put inside jit.

QualificationConfig controls value and derivative tolerances and the finite-difference step. Defaults assume double precision. For float32, choose larger tolerances and a larger step appropriate to the state/direction scales; roundoff and cancellation can spoil a derivative comparison. A value-correct reference with a wrong derivative is caught by the directional check.

The derivative helper is qualified for JAX state directions. A direction requested on NumPy or Torch produces an explicit unqualified check; this utility does not promise identical AD transforms across every backend. See the backend capability matrix for compiler contracts.

Agreement at selected fixtures is not a proof across all parameter regimes, scientific validity, or solution accuracy of an integrator. Include varied fixtures, boundary cases, meaningful balance conditions, and independent domain-specific evidence for the conclusions you need.

docs.title: Derived scalar balance artifacts
docs.text: Conditional reaction balances export exact incidence identities, explicit source terms and coverage/assumptions for a bounded scalar model. They are distinct from user-supplied InvariantCheck callbacks and do not replace independent numerical/runtime qualification. Unsupported spatial, operator or incomplete dynamics produce no issued laws rather than a partial model being treated as the whole system.

docs.title: Operator metadata
docs.text: op_system validates operators as model-level metadata and publishes them as typed OperatorDescriptor values. Engines own spatial discretization and solver staging, but they must agree on the meaning of the descriptor.

docs.title: Advection and transport
docs.text:
Advection acts along the declared coordinate order. With no direction, velocity is signed: positive moves toward increasing indices and negative moves toward decreasing indices.

Use direction when the orientation is structural but the non-negative coefficient remains dynamic:

operators:
  - kind: advection
    axis: imm
    velocity: waning_rate
    direction: decreasing
    bc: reflecting

Providers multiply an increasing coefficient by +1 and a decreasing coefficient by -1. Numeric or traced coefficients supplied with a direction should therefore be non-negative.

Boundary conditions are relative to the resolved direction:

  • absorbing: zero upstream inflow and free downstream outflow;
  • reflecting: zero upstream inflow and zero downstream flux, with mass accumulating in the terminal cell;
  • periodic: downstream outflow wraps to the upstream cell.

These rules apply identically for increasing and decreasing transport. The descriptor keeps direction separate from a parameter name so engines never need to parse backend-specific scalar expressions such as -waning_rate.

docs.title: Jump integrals
docs.text:
jump_integral is a conservative gain-minus-loss operator along one axis. Its matrix uses rows as sources and columns as targets. Given a non-negative off-diagonal rate-density matrix J, op_system defines a generator Q by masking disallowed destinations and setting each diagonal to the negative off-diagonal row sum. Engines apply

[ \frac{d x}{d t}\bigg|_{jump} = r\,xQ ]

along the declared axis. The scalar rate r is separate so it can remain a dynamic inference parameter.

operators:
  - kind: jump_integral
    axis: trait
    rate: jump_rate
    direction: up
    bc: reflecting
    kernel:
      form: matrix
      params: {matrix: trait_jump_density}
      param_axes: {trait_jump_density: [trait, trait]}

The current contract intentionally has one kernel form, matrix. Unknown forms are rejected. The matrix diagonal must be zero and off-diagonal values must be finite and non-negative. kernel.param_axes is mandatory and must declare [axis, axis]; this fixes orientation and lets providers request the parameter with the correct shape.

Directions are defined in declared coordinate order:

  • up retains source-to-target entries with target > source;
  • down retains entries with target < source;
  • both retains every off-diagonal entry and is the default.

Categorical axes are unordered and therefore accept only both. Ordinal axes use their listed order. Continuous axes require strictly increasing numeric coordinates and multiply each target column by the axis's trapezoidal quadrature weight. Thus a continuous kernel has rate-density units inverse to the axis units, while rate * J * target_weight has inverse-time units.

Only reflecting boundaries are defined. This means truncation at the declared domain: no jump outside the coordinate set occurs, the remaining in-domain off-diagonal rates are not renormalized, and a terminal source with no allowed target has a zero generator row. Every row sums to zero, so mass is conserved for every independent slice of the other state axes. absorbing and periodic are rejected until their non-local geometry is specified.

jump_integral_generator, jump_integral_rhs, and validate_jump_integral_kernel are public Array-API reference functions. Engines must match them exactly. Validate concrete parameter values at an eager orchestration boundary; the reference assembly itself keeps matrix values dynamic for JAX, Torch, and other differentiable array backends.

The older project-local Diffrax behavior that treated kernel.params as per-coordinate diagonal outflow is not this operator: it omitted direction and required a separately duplicated inflow. Model that behavior as an explicit source transition, or migrate it to the conservative matrix contract.

docs.title: Parameter declarations
docs.text:
An optional parameters block records scientific annotations for parameters already inferred from the RHS. It does not introduce symbols, supply values, enforce runtime bounds, select an inference library or change the equations. Specs without this block keep their existing behavior.

kind: expr
state: [x]
equations:
  x: "offset - rate*x"
parameters:
  rate:
    support: positive
    units: "day^-1"
    description: "Loss rate"
    fixed: false
  offset:
    support: {kind: bounded, lower: 0, upper: 10}
    units: "amount/day"
    fixed: true

Each entry is optional, as is each field within an entry. An omitted support stays unknown; it is not inferred as real. Undeclared RHS parameters remain valid. Unknown declaration fields and names that are not inferred runtime parameters are errors. Values and priors belong in the caller or statistical layer, outside this block.

Field Meaning support real, strict positive (x > 0), closed unit_interval (0 <= x <= 1), or a bounded mapping support.kind: bounded Requires finite numeric lower < upper; both endpoints are included units Nonempty text annotation; no dimensional-analysis proof is implied description Nonempty human-readable text fixed Boolean inference annotation, default false; it neither binds a value nor removes a runtime argument

The same block is supported for expression and transition specs. Declare a shaped or time-varying buffer by its base name, such as rate, rather than rate[unit] or a coordinate-expanded cell name. Alias-only parameter dependencies are included. States, axes and compiler-synthesized masks are not parameters that this block can declare. Operator-only coefficients and initial-state-only inputs are outside this RHS declaration interface.

Compilation exposes a detached read-only mapping, CompiledRhs.param_meta, whose values are immutable ParameterDeclaration records. Their optional support values are ParameterSupport records. Both types are exported by op_system and op_system.specs. Metadata survives compiled-object pickle round trips by recompiling its normalized source.

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "state": ["x"],
    "equations": {"x": "-rate*x"},
    "parameters": {"rate": {"support": "positive", "fixed": True}},
})
assert compiled.param_meta["rate"].fixed
support = compiled.param_meta["rate"].support
assert support is not None and support.kind == "positive"
np.testing.assert_allclose(compiled.eval_fn(0.0, np.array([3.0]), rate=0.5), [-1.5])

Downstream tools decide how to use these declarations, including support validation, fixed-value binding, prior selection and coordinate transforms. For example, a logit transform covers the interior of a closed unit interval; endpoint atoms require their own statistical treatment. Array namespace, dtype and differentiation behavior remain properties of the numerical evaluation, independent of these static annotations.

Named latent observables can infer additional scalar or shaped parameters and annotate them in this same parameters block. Those names appear in param_meta and in each observable's parameter_shapes, while the existing RHS binding requirements and param_names remain unchanged.

docs.title: Conditional balances from scalar reactions
docs.text:
reaction_balances(compiled) derives exact integer coordinate-sum identities from named scalar unit-transfer reactions. It does not evaluate propensities or change the compiled equations. The report distinguishes represented closed transfers, explicit external sources, unsupported contributions and scientific applicability conditions.

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec, reaction_balances

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "transitions",
    "state": ["a", "b"],
    "transitions": [
        {"name": "transfer", "from": "a", "to": "b", "rate": "k"},
        {"name": "inflow", "to": "a", "rate": "q"},
    ],
})
report = reaction_balances(compiled)
law = report.laws[0]
assert report.fully_covered
assert law.coefficients == (1, 1)
assert not law.closed
assert law.sources[0].reaction_name == "inflow"
assert law.sources[0].coefficient == 1

derivative = compiled.eval_fn(0.0, np.asarray([2.0, 3.0]), k=0.2, q=0.5)
np.testing.assert_allclose(np.dot(law.coefficients, derivative), 0.5)
# The identity is d(a + b)/dt = q, not a closed conservation law.

Removing the inflow transition gives a closed coordinate total. Changing its rate, its time dependence or the state dependence of the internal transfer does not change the incidence identity. An isolated state receives its own constant-coordinate law when it has no represented source or transfer.

Supplied model fully_covered Issued law Complete scalar unit transfers True Closed component totals Those transfers plus source-only reactions True Explicit open balances for affected components Omitted, unsupported or inconsistent dynamics False No laws; inspect coverage_gaps

docs.title: Exact derivation and recorded meaning
docs.text:
An internal column has -1 at its consumed state and +1 at its target. The condition c.T @ S_internal = 0 therefore requires equal coefficients on states joined by a transfer. Indicators of the undirected connected components form an exact integer basis. The implementation traverses this graph without adding a symbolic/SVD dependency or selecting a numerical rank tolerance. This conclusion depends on the unit-transfer contract; it does not generalize to arbitrary molecular stoichiometry or all nonlinear first integrals.

Every coefficient vector follows report.state_names. Component names follow compiled first-state order and are stable within that report; they are not persistent identities across revised models. reaction_names records every covered channel. Each ReactionBalanceSource names a source-only channel, its target and its integer propensity multiplier. Resolve its numerical flux using the matching compiled reaction/parameters. The records contain no callbacks or parameter values and can be inspected, hashed and pickled.

origin="compiled_unit_transfers" records the derivation method. It differs from a user-authored InvariantCheck and from a numerical residual check. The report is a conditional structural artifact, without authenticated provenance or a claim about an arbitrary replacement runtime callback.

docs.title: Scientific metadata and coverage
docs.text:
state_meta and axis_meta are detached tuples of immutable declaration records. Missing units or representation labels remain unknown. Each law and report includes applicability assumptions: summed coordinates need compatible units/representations, and execution must faithfully realize these channels without additional state updates, fluxes, clipping, projections, resets or impulses. Unit labels are compared for known component conflicts; no dimensional analysis or unit conversion is performed. Disconnected components can carry different unit labels.

A numeric coordinate sum is not automatically a physical mass or spatial integral. Intensive quantities need their physical measures before making that interpretation; no mesh weights are inferred here. Use state representations and numerical qualification for declared measures and independent runtime checks.

This first analysis requires scalar templates and complete, uniquely named reaction artifacts matching normalized transition identities. Original ReactionGap records retain their origin and selectors inside BalanceCoverageGap. Templated/routed/shifted/spatial layouts, operators, unknown or duplicate identities, missing artifacts, known conflicting scientific labels, and declared sources/couplings/constraints blocks (including empty reserved blocks) prevent all issued laws. Unsupported contributions are never assigned zero flux. Reaction reactant/dependency completeness is a separate contract: it constrains some stochastic methods, while this analysis uses the represented net unit-transfer columns.

Weighted spatial balances, boundary/operator fluxes and more general stoichiometric derivations are not implemented by this analysis. The analysis leaves normalized/compiled storage and numerical evaluation unchanged, and adds no engine, framework or statistical dependency.

docs.title: Renewal births into a pinned age bin
docs.text:
A source-only transition (from: null, or omitted from) adds its rate to the destination without depleting a donor. Its rate is a total flux, rather than a per-capita coefficient multiplied by the destination population. It may reduce states and age-indexed parameters over an axis that is pinned on the destination.

import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec

spec = {
    "kind": "transitions",
    "axes": [{"name": "age", "coords": ["a0", "a1", "a2"]}],
    "state": ["N[age]", "M[age]"],
    "transitions": [
        {
            "name": "renewal",
            "from": None,
            "to": "N[age=a0]",
            "rate": "sum_over(B[age:a] * (N[age:a] + M[age:a]), age=a)",
            "reactants": [],
        }
    ],
}
compiled = compile_spec(spec)
state = {"N": np.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0]), "M": np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])}
fertility = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
births = fertility @ (state["N"] + state["M"])
assert compiled.pytree_eval_fn is not None
drift = compiled.pytree_eval_fn(0.0, state, B=fertility)
np.testing.assert_allclose(drift["N"], [births, 0.0, 0.0])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(drift["M"], np.zeros(3))

(reaction,) = compiled.reactions
assert reaction.from_base is None
assert reaction.from_axes == reaction.to_axes == ()
assert reaction.full_axes == ("age",)
assert reaction.pinned == (("age", 0),)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    np.asarray(reaction.propensity_fn(0.0, state, B=fertility)), births
)

Here a is a local reduction variable. The bracket form age:a binds the state or parameter position to that variable; it does not create a free reaction-channel axis. sum_over(B[age] * N[age], age=age) also binds age locally and counts the resulting flux once. Unknown reduction axes raise InvalidRhsSpecError.

Named transitions publish a reaction artifact. With every destination axis pinned, the artifact has one scalar propensity: one Poisson stream into the specified cell. The rate already contains the population dependence; a consumer must apply only the destination increment for each firing. The explicit reactants: [] declares that no population is consumed by a birth. It does not imply that the rate is independent of population. With reactants: auto instead, a birth rate such as sum_over(B[age:a] * N[age:a], age=a) publishes no reactants, its dependencies (every N cell it reads), and propensity_order: 1, which is what adaptive tau-leaping needs to bound how fast the hazard can change.

If a group axis remains free, for example to: N[age=a0,group] with rate sum_over(B[age:a] * N[age:a,group], age=a), the propensity has one entry per group. The age reduction happens within each group; from_axes and to_axes are both ("group",), while full_axes retains the destination's full axis order. Bound variables inside aliases have the same scope. An unreduced free axis outside the channel axes remains outside the reaction-artifact contract. For example, multiplying this pinned birth flux by B[age] without reducing that occurrence introduces an extra free age dimension.

The flat RHS, PyTree RHS, and reaction propensity use the same flux. The flepimop2 provider publishes the artifact through system.option("reactions") and the shaped RHS through system.option("pytree_stepper_fn"). Both support NumPy and JAX arrays, including runtime state and parameter changes under JAX tracing.

docs.title: A stationary living population
docs.text:
Births alone increase total population. Conservation of the living total requires balancing departures. The following three-bin model has renewal births, aging, and constant per-capita mortality mu. D is an absorbing counter of departures, so its derivative is positive even when the living population is stationary.

The bins represent [0, h), [h, 2h), and the open-ended tail [2h, infinity). For a constant aging hazard g, the stationary living proportions are (1-q, q*(1-q), q**2), where q = g/(g+mu). Setting g = mu/expm1(mu*h) makes these exactly the bin integrals of the normalized continuum density mu*exp(-mu*a). This is an exponential-fitted aging rate. The usual upwind rate g = 1/h instead gives a discrete geometric profile that approaches the continuum profile as h decreases.

import math

import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec

spec = {
    "kind": "transitions",
    "axes": [{"name": "age", "coords": ["a0", "a1", "a2"]}],
    "state": ["N[age]", "D[age]"],
    "transitions": [
        {
            "name": "renewal",
            "from": None,
            "to": "N[age=a0]",
            "rate": "sum_over(B[age:a] * N[age:a], age=a)",
            "reactants": [],
        },
        {
            "name": "depart",
            "from": "N[age]",
            "to": "D[age]",
            "rate": "mu",
            "reactants": [{"state": "N[age]", "order": 1}],
        },
        *(
            {
                "name": f"age_{k}",
                "from": f"N[age=a{k}]",
                "to": f"N[age=a{k + 1}]",
                "rate": "aging",
                "reactants": [{"state": f"N[age=a{k}]", "order": 1}],
            }
            for k in range(2)
        ),
    ],
}
mu, h, total = 0.2, 1.0, 1000.0
q = math.exp(-mu * h)
population = total * np.array([1.0 - q, q * (1.0 - q), q**2])
params = {
    "mu": np.asarray(mu),
    "aging": np.asarray(mu / math.expm1(mu * h)),
    "B": np.full(3, mu),
}
compiled = compile_spec(spec)
assert compiled.pytree_eval_fn is not None
drift = compiled.pytree_eval_fn(0.0, {"N": population, "D": np.zeros(3)}, **params)
np.testing.assert_allclose(drift["N"], np.zeros(3), atol=1e-12)
np.testing.assert_allclose(drift["D"], mu * population)

The last living bin has no aging outflow because it represents the entire tail, rather than a truncated finite age interval. Constant fertility B = mu makes births equal total living departures at any state. Thus sum(dN/dt) = 0 for arbitrary living populations, while the stationary profile also makes each individual living-bin derivative zero.

For a stochastic consumer, these are population-dependent birth and death hazards with zero expected total living-population drift. Individual paths still fluctuate and can become extinct; the departure counter is excluded from the living total and age distribution. The ensemble stationarity check belongs in the numerical engine's integration tests.

docs.title: Scaling gauges
docs.text:
Available in OP System 0.9.0. The complete example file is included in the source checkout.

A positive scaling action can change state/parameter units while leaving the model's observed outputs unchanged. Declare it next to the equations, verify it at compilation, and optionally bind scalar parameters to select one representative. This analysis concerns deterministic equations and outputs; it does not establish structural identifiability.

"""Verify a shared scaling and map to a fixed representative."""

import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec

SPEC = {
    "kind": "expr",
    "state": ["x"],
    "equations": {"x": "rate*x*(1-x/K)"},
    "observables": {"fraction": {"expr": "x/K"}},
    "gauges": [{"name": "units", "states": {"x": 1}, "parameters": {"K": 1}}],
}
model = compile_spec(SPEC, detect_gauges=True, gauge_fix={"K": 1.0})
assert model.gauges is not None  # ruff: ignore[assert]
assert model.gauges.rank == 1  # ruff: ignore[assert]
assert model.gauge_fix is not None  # ruff: ignore[assert]
natural = np.array([6.0])
coordinates = model.gauge_fix.encode(natural, {"rate": 0.5, "K": 12.0})
assert coordinates.valid  # ruff: ignore[assert]
np.testing.assert_allclose(coordinates.state, [0.5])
assert coordinates.parameters == {"rate": 0.5}  # ruff: ignore[assert]
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    model.eval_fn(0, coordinates.state, **coordinates.parameters), [0.125]
)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    model.observables["fraction"].eval_fn(0, coordinates.state), 0.5
)
state, parameters = model.gauge_fix.decode(coordinates)
np.testing.assert_allclose(state, natural)
assert np.isclose(parameters["K"], 12)  # ruff: ignore[assert]

For this example, replacing x and K by s*x and s*K, with s > 0, multiplies dx/dt by s and preserves the output x/K. Choosing K = 1 uses x/K as the state in the fixed representative.

Quantity Original values Fixed representative State x 6 0.5 Scale parameter K 12 1, bound at compilation Rate 0.5 0.5 Derivative 1.5 0.125 Observed fraction 0.5 0.5

Use gauge_fix.encode(initial_state, original_parameters) for each original parameter draw and check its native valid flag. Integrate the returned state using the fixed model and remaining parameters. The model rejects runtime overrides of its anchors. Its flat, PyTree, block-PyTree and observable interfaces bind the same constants. Scalar anchors may occur only in the observation model. param_names and observable parameter shapes omit bound anchors; available parameter declarations mark them fixed.

encode requires real floating states and scalar, positive anchors. It has no hidden floor or clamp. Separate draws can be mapped with JAX vmap; the map and evaluators also have NumPy and CPU PyTorch checks, with native AD checks where supported. Remaining shaped parameters retain their arrays. One scale is shared across every coordinate of a named state/parameter base. This does not introduce one free generator per cell.

A quotient alone cannot reconstruct the discarded scale. decode takes the full GaugeCoordinates, including the original group coordinates, to recover that original state and parameter point. Retain these coordinates if an inverse map is needed. Pickling a compiled model retains its analysis/fixing options and rebuilds the evaluators.

docs.title: Verification and detection
docs.text:
Compiling declared gauges probes RHS covariance and every declared observable's invariance. A failed comparison raises a diagnostic naming the gauge/output. CompiledRhs.gauges.verification records the seed (19471), four points per generator, positive scales (0.5 and 2), relative tolerance 1e-9, absolute tolerance 1e-11, checked outputs and largest absolute residual. Points use positive uniform state/parameter values in [0.6, 1.4] and times in [0.1, 0.9]; unscaled bounded parameters are sampled inside their support. Finite probes are not a proof across a continuous domain.

detect_gauges=True additionally constructs rational homogeneity constraints from supported expression structure and computes an exact integer nullspace. It handles supported monomials, additive degree matching, ratios, powers and homogeneous reductions, along with specified native math rules. The report separates detected directions from declarations and records whether those rules also verify the declarations. Detection is conservative: identities requiring algebraic cancellation can hide additional directions. Unsupported operations fail an explicit detection request rather than reporting an empty group. Ordinary undeclared compilation does not run this analysis; gauges is None, which differs from an analyzed rank-zero action.

rank is the reported action's rank on states and parameters together; parameter_rank is its parameter projection. Duplicate generators do not increase rank. invariant_coordinates contains integer-exponent monomials in shared parameter bases. These monomials need not be a complete coordinate basis for shaped arrays, whose within-array ratios can carry more invariants. The anchored map transforms the complete arrays and retains their entries. Neither these ranks nor the monomial count is an identifiable-dimension estimate.

docs.title: Assumptions and limits
docs.text:
The action must transform initial states along with parameters. Known initial conditions, priors or other observations can remove a freedom even if the RHS is covariant. Preset initial_state specifications are rejected during fixing: remove that preset and explicitly encode it with its original parameter values. A fixed or bounded parameter cannot participate in the reported global positive scaling action. Anchors must be rank-many independent scalar parameters with finite positive targets; invariant declared outputs are required for fixing.

Named-axis fields and expression-based nonlocal reductions can participate in the shared action when their operations have supported homogeneity rules. Separate operator descriptors, history providers and time tables require additional scaling contracts and are rejected by this analysis. This prevents an instantaneous RHS check from being presented as verification of omitted dynamics. Ordinary compilation of those model classes remains available.

Gauge-fixed models omit stochastic reaction exports and report gauge_fix_requires_jump_contract gaps. Deterministic drift covariance alone does not preserve a jump process's distribution; changing state units also changes the meaning of a unit jump. A stochastic consumer must reject these gaps. A declared but unfixed model retains its original natural-state reactions.

docs.title: Validation reports
docs.text:
python -m op_system.validate model.yml --detect-gauges --json
python -m op_system.validate model.yml --gauge-fix K=1

Repeat --gauge-fix for independent anchors. CLI options apply to each selected specification. validate_spec accepts the same keyword options and reports counts under gauges. Parameter-coordinate counts after removing the reported action describe a generic nonzero parameter point. Missing symmetries, fixed initial conditions and observation assumptions still require separate analysis; the report explicitly leaves identifiability unassessed. Counts cover equation and declared-observable parameters; free initial-condition seeds or noise-model parameters supplied elsewhere are outside this count.

The report's parameters mapping continues to describe equation/operator inputs. Observable-only arguments are listed in each compiled observable's parameter shapes; the gauge parameter count includes them.

docs.title: State representations and physical measures
docs.text:
An optional state_metadata block describes state values. Declarations use state base names, such as rho for rho[space], and work in expression and transition specifications. Partial declarations are allowed. Metadata leaves equations, runtime values, constraints and existing reductions unchanged.

The optional scale: log field requests a separate deterministic coordinate view. It leaves the primary evaluator and stochastic reactions in physical coordinates; callers explicitly encode initial states and select the view's callbacks.

kind: expr
axes:
  - name: space
    type: continuous
    coords: [0.05, 0.25, 0.7]
    units: m
    measure:
      kind: cell
      weights: [0.1, 0.3, 0.6]
      units: m
state: ["rho[space]", "mass[space]", counter]
equations:
  rho[space]: "0"
  mass[space]: "0"
  counter: "sum_state()"
state_metadata:
  rho:
    representation: density
    units: items/m
    description: Cell-average density on the unit interval
    measure_axes: [space]
  mass:
    representation: counts
    units: items
    measure_axes: []
  counter:
    representation: cumulative
    units: items

The illustrative counter derivative exposes the existing total reduction; choose scientific counter equations explicitly in an actual model.

Representation Stored value Physical total over represented cells counts Extensive count per cell/category Unweighted sum cell_mass Extensive amount or mass per cell Unweighted sum density Amount per declared spatial measure Sum after multiplying by that measure concentration Amount per declared volume or reference measure Sum after multiplying by that measure cumulative Extensive accumulated counter Unweighted spatial sum; time differences require a separately defined observation

Counts are annotations, rather than an integer execution constraint. cumulative neither proves monotonic equations nor turns an instantaneous derivative into an interval count. Missing representation remains unknown. For intensive states, omitted measure_axes means integration requirements are undeclared; [] explicitly requires no measure axes. Listed axes must belong to the state template or its legacy state_axes declaration and have explicit measures. Extensive representations reject nonempty measure_axes to avoid weighting an amount twice.

CompiledRhs.state_meta is a read-only mapping from declared bases to exported immutable StateDeclaration records; undeclared bases are absent. CompiledRhs.axis_meta contains all declared axes as AxisDeclaration records with coordinate units and optional AxisMeasure. Undeclared units/measures are None, including on continuous axes. Trusted pickle round trips rebuild the detached snapshots alongside the evaluator.

Supported measure kinds are:

  • counting: unit weight per coordinate; omit weights.
  • cell: explicit cell widths, areas or volumes aligned with coordinates.
  • quadrature: explicit point weights aligned with coordinates.

Cell/quadrature weights must match the coordinate count and be finite, strictly positive real numbers. Boolean, zero, negative and nonfinite weights fail. Signed quadrature, zero-measure masks, runtime measure buffers and nonseparable multidimensional geometry are outside this initial interface. Coordinate and measure units are independent: coordinates may use m while volumes use m^3. Annotations do not verify dimensions or geometry.

The discretization owner supplies the measure. It is never inferred from centers or substituted for existing continuous-axis deltas. Those deltas retain point-trapezoidal semantics over the coordinate span. Centers [0.05, 0.25, 0.7] span 0.65; the declared volumes [0.1, 0.3, 0.6] cover the unit interval. These describe different discretizations.

This runnable example explicitly reduces a density using the exported measure:

import numpy as np
from op_system import array_namespace, compile_spec

compiled = compile_spec({
    "axes": [
        {
            "name": "space",
            "type": "continuous",
            "coords": [0.05, 0.25, 0.7],
            "measure": {"kind": "cell", "weights": [0.1, 0.3, 0.6], "units": "m"},
        }
    ],
    "state": ["rho[space]"],
    "equations": {"rho[space]": "0"},
    "state_metadata": {
        "rho": {
            "representation": "density",
            "units": "items/m",
            "measure_axes": ["space"],
        }
    },
})
density = np.asarray([1.1, 1.5, 2.4])  # Cell averages of 1+2*x on [0,1].
xp = array_namespace(density)
measure = compiled.axis_meta["space"].measure
assert measure is not None
weights = xp.asarray(measure.weights, dtype=density.dtype)
cell_counts = xp.multiply(density, weights)
physical_total = xp.sum(cell_counts)  # 2: exact integral over [0,1].
unweighted_density_total = xp.sum(density)  # 5: a different quantity.

These operations preserve NumPy/JAX/Torch namespace and floating dtype; required backend qualification executes their numerical expectations. Metadata supplies no new expression helper: sum_state() remains unweighted, and existing integration helpers retain their point weights. Named latent observables can describe measured quantities. Numerical consumers must check representation, measure coverage, unit assumptions and actual discretization accuracy before interpreting an observable as a physical integral or conserved quantity. This metadata does not implement mesh transfer.

Existing specs need no migration. When annotating a state, review whether its values are extensive or intensive and supply the measure explicitly. This interface does not convert representations, constrain signs or counters, or certify scientific validity.

Use named latent observables to compile these explicit physical reductions into independently discoverable fixed-mesh outputs.

Conditional scalar reaction balances retain these declarations without inferring physical mass or spatial weights. Known unit or representation conflicts within a proposed total remain visible coverage gaps; unknown labels remain assumptions.

docs.title: Time-indexed parameters
docs.text:
A parameter subscripted with the configured time axis is supplied as a table. For example, rate[time] takes one value per declared time coordinate, while rate[group,time] takes one table per group. The compiler removes the time dimension at each evaluation and passes the resulting scalar or shaped value to the equations and reaction propensities. The time axis can occupy any position in the parameter array; its coordinate order defines the table order.

The top-level time_interpolation field chooses one policy for all time-indexed parameters in the specification:

Policy Value between adjacent coordinates linear Linear interpolation; the default when the field is omitted previous Hold the value at t_i on [t_i, t_{i+1})

Both policies clamp to the nearest endpoint outside the coordinate range. previous is right-continuous: evaluating exactly at a coordinate returns the new table value. For coordinates [0, 1, 2] and values [0, 3, 1], evaluations at 0.5, 1, and 1.5 return [0, 3, 3] with previous and [1.5, 3, 2] with linear.

import numpy as np

from op_system import compile_spec

spec = {
    "kind": "transitions",
    "time_interpolation": "previous",
    "axes": [
        {"name": "group", "coords": ["a"]},
        {"name": "time", "type": "continuous", "coords": [0.0, 1.0, 2.0]},
    ],
    "state": ["A[group]", "B[group]"],
    "transitions": [
        {
            "name": "transfer",
            "from": "A[group]",
            "to": "B[group]",
            "rate": "rate[time]",
            "reactants": [{"state": "A[group]", "order": 1}],
        }
    ],
}
compiled = compile_spec(spec)
table = np.asarray([0.0, 3.0, 1.0])
drift = compiled.eval_fn(1.5, np.asarray([10.0, 0.0]), rate=table)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(drift, [-30.0, 30.0])
assert compiled.meta["forcing_breakpoints"] == (1.0, 2.0)

Use time_axis: day with a declared day axis and subscripts such as rate[day] to rename the time axis. Active time coordinates must be finite, numeric, and strictly increasing. A continuous time axis may explicitly declare a single coordinate; its table is constant for every evaluation time. Other continuous axes retain their requirement for at least two coordinates. Unknown policy values are rejected during normalization.

Flat, PyTree, block, and reaction evaluators use the same policy. They adopt tables into the evolving state's namespace at call time, including JAX under jit and vmap. Runtime table values are not baked into compiled functions.

docs.title: Metadata for numerical engines
docs.text:
Normalized and compiled metadata expose time_axis, time_interpolation, time_coordinates, and forcing_breakpoints. Coordinates and breakpoints are immutable tuples. The flepimop2 system provider exposes the same four values through system.option(...).

For an active previous table, forcing breakpoints are all coordinates after the first. The first coordinate introduces no change because the first table value also applies before it. A single-coordinate table has no breakpoints. Linear interpolation and specifications without active time-indexed parameters publish an empty breakpoint tuple.

An engine can pass the published forcing boundaries to its breakpoint-aware stochastic solver independently of the observation grid. In op_engine, pure stochastic direct SSA, fixed tau-leaping, and adaptive tau-leaping accept forcing_breakpoints. The flepimop2-op_engine 0.7.0 provider automatically merges the producer schedule with explicitly supplied forcing boundaries. Other consumers must wire these metadata into their solver configuration. The interpolation setting changes table evaluation only. A rate that also uses t directly can still vary between table coordinates. Exact breakpoint SSA and adaptive exact fallback require all external time dependence to be constant between declared changes while the state is unchanged.

Linear tables continue to produce smoothly varying rates. Listing their coordinates as breakpoints does not make frozen-rate SSA exact; those rates require a suitable time-dependent waiting-time method.
